questions.question: A 19-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with multiple episodes of unexplained abdominal pain. He also has documented positive faecal occult bloods. On examination, there is peri-oral pigmentation with a number of macular lesions which cross the vermillion border. His blood pressure (BP) is normal at 110/70 mmHg, while his pulse is 68 beats per minute (bpm) and his body mass index (BMI) is 23 kg/m². His abdomen is soft but mildly tender on palpation. He is admitted to the Emergency Department (ED) acutely a few days later after an upper gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage. An upper GI endoscopy reveals a number of hamartomatous polyps. Which of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
questions.explanation:
B. Peutz-Jegher's syndrome

This is an autosomal dominant disorder characterised by the presence of multiple hamartomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract, and mucocutaneous melanocytic macules. The condition has equal sex distribution and has been documented in most races. The cause is thought to be a mutation of the serine threonine kinase 11 gene. There is significant risk of eventual malignant transformation. Almost half of all Peutz-Jegher's syndrome patients develop and die from cancer by the age of 57 years. The mean age at first diagnosis of cancer is 43 years. The cumulative risks of cancer development are highest for the stomach, colon, pancreas and breast. Regular surveillance examinations, endoscopies and ultrasound imaging (yearly) are recommended.

C. Gardener's syndrome

Gardener's syndrome leads to formation of multiple adenomas, and is associated with the development of colon cancer. It is also associated with multiple osteomas, skin and soft tissue tumours.

A. Plummer-Vinson syndrome

Plummer Vinson syndrome is characterized by difficulty in swallowing, iron deficiency anaemia, glossitis, angular cheilosis (also known as angular cheilitis) and oesophageal webs. It is a risk factor for development of squamous cell carcinoma.

D. Familial adenomatous polyposis

FAP is associated with colonic polyps and increased risk of colon cancer, without the peri-oral pigmentation seen here.

E. Cowden disease

Cowden's disease is associated with formation of multiple hamartomatous polyps, it causes oral mucosal papillomatosis and acral keratoses, rather than the picture seen here.

questions.question:
A 73-year-old man who is confined to bed for most of the day because of a right-sided hemiplegic stroke, is admitted on the Emergency Department (ED) with a sacral pressure sore. His General Practitioner (GP) and Practice Nurse have been keeping it dressed, although it has continued to deteriorate and he is now pyrexial and confused. On examination, he is pyrexial - his temperature is 38.5°C. His blood pressure (BP) is 105/70 mmHg, while his pulse is 92 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. There is a 5 cm sacral pressure sore with a necrotic edge. There is frank pus within the wound itself. Investigations reveal the following;

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)109 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)15.2 × 10⁹/l4.0-11.0 × 10⁹/l
Platelets (PLT)201 × 10⁹/l150-400 × 10⁹/l
Sodium (Na+)137 mmol/l135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)4.5 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)132 µmol/l50-120 µmol/l
C-reactive protein (CRP)201 mg/l< 10 mg/l
Glucose8.4 mmol/l (fasting)< 5.6 mmol/l

Which of the following is the most important intervention?
questions.explanation:
E. Surgical debridement

The answer is Surgical debridement - At this stage signs of significant systemic bacteraemia, (pyrexia, confusion, elevated white count and marked elevation in CRP), coupled with necrotic tissue around the pressure sore, debridement is the most appropriate next step. This could then be followed by IV antibiotics. Given the glucose indicates diabetes mellitus, a relatively broad-spectrum antibiotic such as Co-amoxiclav should be considered.

B. IV Co-amoxiclav

IV coamoxiclav, is incorrect, but is appropriate as an antibiotic choice, but should be considered in addition to surgical debridement.

A. Hydrogel dressing

Hydrogel dressing, is incorrect however it is appropriate with respect to removing slough / necrotic tissue from the wound, although given significant systemic features of bacteraemia, surgical debridement is the better choice here.

C. Larval therapy

Larval therapy, is incorrect, it is one method of removing necrotic tissue, although more rapid resolution of symptoms with surgical debridement is the better option.

D. Silver nitrate dressing

Silver nitrate dressing, is incorrect, silver based dressings are generally considered for wounds with minimal amounts of slough / necrotic tissue, such as burns, rather than the pressure sore seen here.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department (ED) for review. She is concerned about a suspicious mole on her leg and has recently returned from a six-month working holiday on a farm in Australia. On further questioning, it transpires that she has had extensive sun exposure and has had three moles removed over the past five years. On examination, she is pale-skinned with ginger hair. The mole on her left calf is shown below: Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
B. Excision biopsy

This lesion has irregular pigmentation and borders. Taking into account her previous history, it may be a malignant melanoma. As such, excision biopsy to provide detailed histology is the most appropriate next step.

The excision margins for the biopsy are dependent upon the stage of melanoma, according to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines.

A. Cryotherapy

Cryotherapy is only recommended for lesions that are suspected to be benign. Removal using cryotherapy makes histological interpretation impossible because of tissue destruction.

C. Loop removal

Loop removal is not recommended for the same reasons cryotherapy should not be used. Significant tissue destruction ensues, and it is difficult to ensure adequate resection margin when loop removal is used.

D. Punch biopsy

Punch biopsy may be taken from an area of the mole where less abnormal cells are identified and would not provide evidence of excision margins. It should not therefore be used here.

E. Topical Fluorouracil

This is used in the treatment of solar keratoses and is an inadequate intervention for malignant melanomas which metastasise early.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with itchy, pigmented macules on her trunk and limbs, which has developed over a period of five years. She says they become particularly itchy and red when they are rubbed and when she has a bath or exercises. She denies any wheezing, flushing, diarrhoea, abdominal pain or any other systemic symptoms. She has no significant past medical history. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
C. Urticaria pigmentosa

Urticaria pigmentosa (UP) or cutaneous mastocytosis is part of a group of conditions called 'mastocytosis', in which mast cells proliferate and accumulate in the skin and other organs. UP is a localised form of mastocytosis confined to the skin. It manifests in brown, freckle-like macules that urticate (become erythematous and raised) if rubbed.

E. Leukaemia cutis

Leukaemia cutis would normally present with more pronounced, raised lesions (papules/nodules or plaques) and one would expect symptoms and signs of bone marrow failure.

A. Vasculitis

Vasculitis is limited to the skin only, and without progression over the course of 5 years to involve other organs such as the kidneys would be very unusual.

B. Systemic mastocytosis

In systemic mastocytosis, mast cells disseminate widely in the skin and there may be systemic symptoms of mast cell release including wheezing, flushing, diarrhoea, hypotension, syncope, dyspnoea and anaphylaxis.

Serum tryptase may be raised.

D. Carcinoid syndrome

Carcinoid syndrome may cause episodic facial flushing eventually leading to persistent facial erythema and telangiectasia. 38520

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with a three day history of painful genital ulceration. The pain is worse on passing urine. She also complains of flu-like symptoms with myalgia and mild fever. On examination, there are multiple small, white painful ulcers all over the genitals. She has tender lymphadenopathy in the inguinal region. A swab is taken of the ulcers. What is the most appropriate next step whilst the results are pending?
options: A. Give 7 days of treatment-dose aciclovir; no further investigations required
B. Take blood for herpes simplex-1 antibodies
C. Take blood for herpes simplex-2 antibodies
D. Take blood for herpes simplex-1 antibodies and give 7 days of treatment-dose acyclovir
E. Take blood for herpes simplex-2 antibodies and give 7 days of treatment-dose aciclovir
questions.explanation:
A. Give 7 days of treatment-dose aciclovir; no further investigations required

This patient has a history and examination consistent with primary genital herpes infection; as such, she should be treated with aciclovir whilst results of swabs to confirm the diagnosis are pending. No blood tests are necessary for the diagnosis: PCR on the viral swabs is sufficient. Treatment is thought to be most effective if initiated in the first 72 hours as complication rates and disease length are both reduced.

D. Take blood for herpes simplex-1 antibodies and give 7 days of treatment-dose acyclovir

It is correct to treat this patient immediately with aciclovir as there is sufficient clinical evidence of genital herpes. However, the PCR from the viral ulcer swabs that have already been taken is sufficient to confirm the diagnosis. There is no need to undertake serological testing, and furthermore, genital herpes is caused by herpes simplex-2, not -1. Serological testing has a poor positive predictive value.

B. Take blood for herpes simplex-1 antibodies

This patient has a history and examination consistent with genital herpes, and should be treated for it whilst confirmation is awaited from PCR on the ulcer swabs. Furthermore, it is herpes simplex-2 that is the most common cause of genital ulceration: herpes simplex-1 typically causes oral ulceration (cold sores). Serology is unhelpful in the diagnosis of herpes virus infections. The correct action would be to give this patient 7 days of treatment-dose aciclovir, and there is no need for further investigation whilst the results of swabs are awaited.

C. Take blood for herpes simplex-2 antibodies

Serology is of very little value in herpes simplex-2 infections: it can take 12 weeks for it to become positive in primary infection, and has a low positive predictive value in low-prevalence populations. The correct course of action would be to give this patient 7 days of treatment-dose aciclovir and await the results of PCR from the viral swabs that have already been taken; there is no need for any further tests.

E. Take blood for herpes simplex-2 antibodies and give 7 days of treatment-dose aciclovir

It is appropriate to give this patient treatment with aciclovir whilst awaiting the results of the swabs, because she has clear clinical features of genital herpes. However, there is no need for serological testing for herpes simplex-2: this has a poor positive predictive value and serology may not be positive until 12 weeks after primary infection. No further investigations are needed in this case: the PCR results from the ulcer swabs are sufficient to confirm the diagnosis and the only action required is to give treatment-dose aciclovir. 71048

questions.question:
An 18-year-old man is reviewed in the Immunology Clinic with a history of recurrent chest infections since infancy. He has recently been seen in the same-day Emergency Care Clinic for left lower limb cellulitis requiring intravenous antibiotics. During the consultation, he also reports visual disturbance, including sensitivity to bright light with occasional blurred vision. He has no known past medical history and recently immigrated to the UK from Eastern Europe. On examination, his observations are within normal limits. There are fine crackles at the lung bases, and his heart sounds are normal. It is noted that his eyes are a pale blue-grey colour, with visible nystagmus on lateral gaze. Trying to assess the pupillary response to light causes significant discomfort to the patient.
InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)135 g/L115–155 g/L
White cell count (WCC)2.7 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils0.4 ×10⁹/L1.8–7.5 ×10⁹/L
Platelets90 ×10⁹/L150–450 ×10⁹/L
Blood filmLysosomal granules within monocytes, granulocytes and leucocytes—
What dermatological condition is most associated with the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Albinism

This patient has a diagnosis of Chédiak-Higashi syndrome. It is a rare autosomal-recessive disease that, due to genetic mutations in the lysosomal trafficking gene, causes recurrent bacterial infections, thrombocytopenia and neurological symptoms including nystagmus, photophobia and peripheral neuropathy. Intellectual disability may also be seen. Characteristic blood film findings include inclusion bodies and lysosomal granules within monocytes, granulocytes and leukocytes, and neutropenia and thrombocytopenia are common. Chédiak- Higashi syndrome is a cause of albinism, a dermatological condition characterised by absent melanin production that leads to general hypopigmentation of the skin, hair and eyes. Pale blue-grey eyes, white or yellow hair and pale skin are all features of albinism, in addition to ocular signs of nystagmus, strabismus and photosensitivity.

B. Erythema nodosum

Erythema nodosum is a hypersensitivity reaction that causes tender and erythematous nodules to appear, most commonly over the shins. It is associated with arthralgia, fever and other underlying conditions, for example, inflammatory bowel disease or sarcoidosis. However, it is not associated with the above presentation.

C. Lichen planus

Lichen planus is an idiopathic inflammatory dermatological condition that causes an eruption of itchy and shiny papules over the extremities that often has a violaceous colour. These lesions are often itchy and can also affect the mucous membranes and genitalia. It is not seen in Chédiak-Higashi syndrome.

D. Pityriasis alba

Pityriasis alba is a hypopigmentation skin condition characterised by multiple small hypopigmented lesions over the face, neck, shoulders and upper arms. It is relatively asymptomatic and may resolve after puberty. It is not related to this patient's presentation.

E. Vitiligo

Vitiligo is a hypopigmentation skin condition associated with underlying autoimmune conditions such as hypothyroidism and pernicious anaemia. The extent of skin involvement in vitiligo ranges from focal skin involvement to complete pigment loss.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a rash in her lower legs, rigors, fever, and a sore throat. A throat swab reveals the presence of gram positive bacteria organised in chains. Which of the following skin conditions is she most likely presenting with?
questions.explanation:
A. Erythema nodosum

Erythema nodosum is a type of panniculitis (inflammation of the adipose tissue) resulting in red, tender nodules, which commonly occur on the lower legs but may also occur anywhere. It is associated with throat infections due to streptococcus or viral infections (as in this case), sarcoidosis, inflammatory bowel disease, tuberculosis and leprosy.

D. Erythema marginatum

Erythema marginatum consists of spreading erythematous rings that are associated with acute rheumatic fever (fever, carditis, migratory polyarthritis,) secondary to infection by group A beta-haemolytic streptococci.

B. Erythema annulare centrifugum

Erythema annulare centrifugum is a chronic, recurrent, annular erythema that may be idiopathic or linked to a number of infections, medications and underlying conditions (e.g. Graves disease).

C. Erythema migrans

Erythema chronicum migrans develops a few days following a tick bite and is a cutaneous pathognomonic sign of Lyme's disease. Expanding, erythematous lesions occur in a bull's-eye pattern and are associated with flu- like symptoms.

E. Erythema induratum

Erythema induratum of Bazin is a rare nodular vasculitis (tender erythematous, indurated nodules and plaques) commonly affecting the posterior calves and associated with mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.

questions.question: A 36-year-old male is refered to the Dermatology Clinic by his General Practitioner (GP) with the on his anterior shoulder shown below. He has a new partner who finds it unsightly and he wants it treated. Which of the following best describes the abnormal area of pigmentation shown on his shoulder?
questions.explanation:
A. Benign epidermal naevus

Benign epidermal naevi, (formerly known as Becker's naevi), have a characteristic appearance with linear pigmentation, often located around the shoulder. They carry a brown pigment due to melanocytes and may also be hairy.

C. Mongolian blue spot

Mongolian blue spots are located over the sacrum, are blue in colour and identified at birth.

B. Naevus flammeus

This is a vascular naevus or port wine stain. When these occur on the head, patients are usually investigated for the presence of leptomeningeal angiomas.

D. Café au lait spot

These are flattened macular pigmented areas identified at birth and associated with neurofibromatosis Type 1.

E. Haemangioma

Haemangiomas are benign vascular tumours identified in childhood, they are known as strawberry naevi because of their colour.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a three month history of itching in the groin region. Her General Practitioner (GP) had prescribed topical steroids for presumed 'eczema'. This has not been of any benefit. The rash is shown below: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Tinea incognito

Tinea is an infection with a dermatophyte fungus. Tinea incognito is the name given to tinea when the clinical appearance has been altered by inappropriate treatment, usually a steroid cream. Compared with untreated tinea corporis, tinea incognito has a less raised margin, is less scaly and more pustular. Treatment with a topical anti-fungal and loose-fitting cotton underwear is likely to resolve the problem.

D. Malassezia furfur

This is the yeast infection thought to be responsible for seborrheic dermatitis and pityriasis versicolor, presenting with a rash on the face or the trunk most commonly.

B. Pthirus pubis

Pubic crabs produce itching and the bites result in wheals and erythematous or bluish macules.

C. Pediculus humanus humanus

This is the body louse, where the lice themselves or their eggs (nits) may be visible.

E. Candida albicans

Candida albicans is more likely to present as an erythematous moist rash with evidence of adherent white discharge. Vulval candidiasis is more likely to be seen than the skin fold/perineal infection seen here.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man body builder presents to the Dermatology Clinic with an itchy rash on his upper left chest, shown below. He maintains that he takes no medication and works out for many hours per day. What is the most likely cause of the rash?
questions.explanation:
D. Anabolic steroid abuse

This is an acneiform eruption consisting of pustules, papules and nodules, and a localised folliculitis on the upper chest. Anabolic steroids are a common cause of iatrogenic acne, and given his body building must be considered a possibility.

C. Body wash

Although an allergic reaction to body wash is possible, a generalised rash rather than the localised changes seen here would be expected.

A. Dermatitis herpetiformis

Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with generalised papules and blisters and often with symptoms of gluten sensitive enteropathy, rather than the localised rash in an otherwise well patient seen here.

B. Tinea corporis

Tinea corporis is seen as a scaly erythematous lesion which gradually enlarges, associated with clearance from the centre.

E. Impetigo

Impetigo is a common skin infection usually occurring on the face, and is associated with honey coloured crusted plaques of infection.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review, following admission to hospital with a third episode of right lower lobe pneumonia in the past two years. He has received several rotating courses of antibiotics from the Community Respiratory Nursing Service and still has a chronic cough, productive of thick, yellow sputum. On examination, there are coarse crackles at both lung bases on auscultation, with wheeze throughout. There is lymphoedema affecting both lower limbs. A picture of his hands is shown below: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his recurrent respiratory tract infections (RTIs)?
questions.explanation:
B. Bronchiectasis

This patient has yellow nail discolouration with nail dystrophy. Coupled with evidence of recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, persistent crackles on auscultation and lymphoedema, the most likely cause of his recurrent respiratory tract infections is bronchiectasis, related to underlying yellow nail syndrome. Pleural effusions are also seen in the condition.

D. Sarcoidosis

Sarcoidosis is associated with hilar lymphadenopathy and, over the longer term, with pulmonary fibrosis in active disease. It does not fit with nail dystrophy, lymphoedema and recurrent respiratory tract infections seen here.

A. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)

We are not given a history of smoking here, and nail dystrophy and lymphoedema, as seen here, are inconsistent with a diagnosis of COPD.

C. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)

GPA is associated with pulmonary infiltration, coupled with evidence of renal vasculitis. It carries an acute presentation, often with evidence of haemoptysis.

E. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)

IPF is associated with crackles on auscultation of the chest, but with finger clubbing, rather than nail dystrophy as seen here.

questions.question: An 18-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with a 1-day history of a non-blanching rash down his legs and buttocks, seen below, and abdominal pain. He has recently been started on antibiotics for a sore throat. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is likely to be present in this patient?
options: A. Deposition of immunoglobulin A (IgA) immune complexes on histology
D. Prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time
questions.explanation:
A. Deposition of immunoglobulin A (IgA) immune complexes on histology

The purpuric rash on the legs with abdominal pain is in keeping with Henoch-Schönlein purpura (HSP).

Perivascular deposits of IgA are characteristic and help to differentiate HSP from other vasculitic disorders.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Purpuraschoenleinhennoch2.JPG

E. Mouth ulcers

Mouth ulceration is not associated with HSP but may be seen in other conditions such as Behcet's disease and Ulcerative colitis.

B. Haematuria

At diagnosis, urinalysis is usually normal, although these can develop over time and haematuria is associated with a risk of future relapse.

C. Thrombocytopenia

Thrombocytopenia is not seen in HSP. The full blood count may show a normochromic anaemia due to recent overt gastrointestinal bleeding.

D. Prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time

Prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) are normal in HSP. When both are prolonged causes include disseminated intravascular coagulation, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency and supratherapeutic doses of warfarin or heparin.

questions.question: An 18-year-old man comes to the Dermatology Clinic having recently returned from a charity visit to a northern Thai beach resort. He has a very itchy 'creeping' eruption on the soles of both his feet. On examination, he has linear tracks on the feet, some of which have secondary blistering, crusting and bacterial infection. A diagnosis of cutaneous larva migrans is made. Which of the following is most likely to harbour the infection?
questions.explanation:
A. Dog

Cutaneous larva migrans is a parasitic skin infection caused by hookworm that usually infect domestic animals such as dogs, cats and sometimes cattle. In the animal host, the larvae penetrate the skin and reach the blood.

They mature in the intestine and lay eggs, which are excreted in the faeces. The larvae are found in beaches and moist soils contaminated with animal faeces. Albendazole and ivermectin are potential interventions.

E. Turkey

Turkeys suffer from caecal worms, which carry the protozoan parasite Histomonas; this leads to death in the turkeys, but isn't a cause of human disease.

B. Fish

Fish tapeworm leads to intestinal infection from uncooked freshwater fish, and is a potential problem with respect to eating sushi.

C. Sand fly

Sand fly bites lead to the development cutaneous leishmaniasis, rather than cutaneous larva migrans.

D. Red ant

Allergic dermatitis may be rarely seen in patients bitten by red ants, although it doesn't lead to the development of cutaneous larva migrans.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. Her main complaint is of unsightly skin changes affecting her neck and axillae. She is under follow-up with the Ophthalmologists after angioid streaks were identified affecting both retinae, and she has been feeling increasingly tired over the past few months. A picture of her right axilla is shown below: Which of the following is she most likely to be suffering from?
questions.explanation:
B. Gastrointestinal haemorrhage

The axillary changes seen in this patient are consistent with pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE), which is also associated with angioid streaks affecting the retina. It is caused by a mutation in the ABCC6 gene, which leads to accumulation of calcium and other minerals in elastic fibres of the skin, eyes and blood vessels. Increasing fragility of blood vessels in the gastrointestinal tract can lead to gastrointestinal haemorrhage, which may account for the tiredness seen here.

E. Lens dislocation

Lens dislocation is associated with Marfan syndrome. Features of Marfan syndrome, including arachnodactyly and recurrent joint dislocation, are absent from this scenario, although angioid streaks are seen in patients with the disease.

A. Aortic stenosis

Aortic stenosis is not a feature of PXE, although both mitral valve prolapse and coronary artery calcification are noted in patients with long-standing disease.

C. Hypothyroidism

Hypothyroidism is not associated with PXE, although PXE may be seen in patients with Down syndrome, which is also associated with hypothyroidism.

D. Interstitial cystitis

Urinary tract haemorrhage is seen in patients with PXE. This is not due to interstitial nephritis; it is usually as a result of vessel fragility.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man is under the care of the Haematology team. He is undergoing chemotherapy for non- Hodgkin's lymphoma. He has been extensively investigated for left-sided chest pain and a recent angiogram demonstrated normal coronaries. On the ward, the nursing staff noticed this rash on his back the previous day: Which of the following medications should be prescribed?
options: B. Aciclovir 800 mg five times daily
D. Morphine sulphate tablets 30 mg BD
questions.explanation:
B. Aciclovir 800 mg five times daily

This gentleman has herpes zoster infection affecting a thoracic dermatome. Herpes zoster occurs in people who have previously had chickenpox. The herpes varicella zoster virus lies dormant in the dorsal root ganglion following chickenpox, and later travels down the cutaneous nerves to infect the epidermal cells. The prodromal period is followed by a rash consisting of a group of vesicles on an erythematous background, followed by weeping and crusting; healing takes 3-4 weeks. The rash is nearly always unilateral and confined to one or two dermatomes. Oral antiviral agents such as aciclovir at a high dose are only beneficial if given in the first 48 h of the development of blisters. Regular analgesics are important, but in the elderly - particularly if given as soon as the rash appears - prophylactic amitriptyline at night starting at 25 mg and increasing to 75 mg can help prevent post-herpetic neuralgia.

D. Morphine sulphate tablets 30 mg BD

Pain relief alone is not appropriate, given that this man is undergoing treatment for Hodgkin's lymphoma and is likely to be immunosuppressed.

A. Flucloxacillin 500 mg QDS

This patient's rash is viral in origin, and flucloxacillin therefore has no value in its management.

C. Topical acyclovir QDS

Topical acyclovir is ineffective in the treatment of herpes zoster, and thus it isn't an optimal intervention here.

E. Prednisolone 30 mg OD

Corticosteroids in this situation may drive persistent or more generalised zoster infection.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a sudden-onset, widespread, erythematous rash, covering 95% of her body. The rash was precipitated by a course of intravenous (IV) vancomycin which has now been discontinued. What would you now expect to happen to this rash?
options: B. Desquamation followed by post-inflammatory pigmentation
D. Complete resolution to normal skin within 3 weeks
questions.explanation:
B. Desquamation followed by post-inflammatory pigmentation

The diagnosis here is exfoliative dermatitis. The erythematous skin begins to desquamate around days 2-6, and this is followed by pigmentation (similar to tanning after sunburn). The pigmentary change (usually hyper- but can be hypo-) can be permanent, or may resolve after a few months.

D. Complete resolution to normal skin within 3 weeks

Pigmentary changes seen after exfoliative dermatitis usually takes a few months to completely resolve.

A. Ulceration

Ulceration is seen in Stevens-Johnson syndrome as it progresses, which doesn't fit with the presentation seen here.

C. Lichenification

Lichenification is a manifestation of chronic pruritic skin disorders driven by recurrent scratching and epidermal hypertrophy, not with the acute erythroderma seen here.

E. Induration and fibrosis

Induration and fibrosis is seen primarily in fibrotic skin diseases such as systemic sclerosis.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man, who is known to suffer with anxiety and depression, presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with an intensely itchy, erythematous patch on his lower leg. He recognises and admits that the rash is worse after itching. There are no other skin problems noted elsewhere. You plan to prescribe an occlusive treatment to help moisturise the skin over the leg. Which of the following is likely to have the most occlusive effect?
questions.explanation:
A. Ointments

Ointments are 80% oil and 20% water. These products feel greasy, do not absorb well and are generally not easy to use on large areas. They are 'occlusive,' which means they trap moisture and heat in very well.

Ointments promote medication absorption over all other formulations.

D. Lotions

Lotions are thinner than creams, they absorb very quickly and feel very light on the skin. They are easier to distribute on hairy areas, but do not retain significant moisture over the skin surface.

B. Gels

Gels are emulsions that contain oil-in-water. They usually have an alcohol base. They dry into a thin, greaseless, film. Like lotions and foams, they are ideal for spreading on hairy areas and large areas.

C. Creams

Creams are a semi-solid emulsion, half oil and half water. This formulation is typically the easiest to use and is preferred by most patients. They spread easily, absorb quickly and wash off with water. They have a medium viscosity, and are reasonably hydrating without feeling too heavy on your skin.

E. Foam

Foams are pressurised collections of gaseous bubbles in a matrix of liquid film. Foam preparations spread readily and are easier to apply than other preparations.

questions.question: A 41-year-old man presents to the General Medical Clinic complaining of changes to his nose which are not subsiding. He has noticed his nose changing in colour without any other symptoms over a period of a few months. Other than this, he has been feeling well in himself. He has a past medical history of a prolapsed lumbar disc and type II diabetes. He takes no regular medications. A photograph of his nose is shown below: Multiple investigations are requested, including routine blood tests, a chest X-ray (CXR), electrocardiogram (ECG) and echocardiogram (ECHO), but no abnormalities are detected. What is the most appropriate medical treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
B. Corticosteroids

This patient has lupus pernio without any other evidence of systemic sarcoidosis. Lupus pernio is a form of cutaneous sarcoidosis which typically presents with an asymptomatic violaceous set of nodules and plaques over the nose, cheek and/or ears. It more commonly affects women and patients of African American descent.

Sarcoidosis is a chronic cell-mediated response to an unknown antigen in which macrophages and CD4 cells release cytokines that cause granulomas to form. Biopsy reveals non-caseating granulomas. In 75% of patients, there is pulmonary involvement, making respiratory investigations important. Treatment for lupus pernio can involve topical or systemic steroids, but sometimes requires systemic treatment such as methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine and biological therapy.

C. Flucloxacillin

Flucloxacillin could be considered for cellulitis or simple bacterial dermatological infections. However, this is typically characterised by an acutely inflamed rash arising over a short time, often with systemic involvement.

The appearance and history do not match this.

A. Topical metronidazole

This would have been an appropriate management option for rhinophyma. Rhinophyma is a condition in which the sebaceous glands of the nose are enlarged with erythema of the nose, as well as overlying telangiectasia.

D. Metformin

Metformin is a first-line medical treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus. Diabetes can present with various dermatological complications such as increase in frequency of cellulitis and necrobiosis lipoidica. The latter is characterised by waxy lesions, but even in such cases improving diabetic control does not remove the lesion.

E. Surgical referral

Surgical referral would be an appropriate consideration if this lesion had appeared malignant. However, such lesions usually present as a single nodule, which is likely to ulcerate. The lack of a specifically defined lesion makes a malignant cause less likely.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a rash on her neck. She has recently been spending time volunteering building a shed with her grandchildren, who noticed the rash. It is erythematous and mildly tender. She has a background of previous deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in her right leg, and atrial fibrillation (AF). She leads an active life and has noted some recent weight loss. After a recent checkup at her General Practitioner (GP) for a rash on her face featuring telangiectasia and pustules, some medication was added. Her medication includes paracetamol, cetirizine, warfarin, bisoprolol, doxycycline and sertraline. A photograph of her skin is shown below: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Doxycycline-induced photosensitivity

This history suggests a photosensitive rash, with the patient spending significant time outside and a rash in a sun-exposed region. All the possible answers suggest photosensitivity. The recent medication change is the key in this answer. The most likely drug in her history to cause photosensitivity is doxycycline , notorious for causing photosensitivity. It is probable that this patient has been started on doxycycline for rosacea. This must be considered most likely in the absence of other systemic symptoms.

C. Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT)

PCT is the most common type of porphyria and is due to a defective enzyme (uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase), leading to a disorder in haematological production. This manifests as fragility of the skin, particularly on the back of the hands, and photosensitivity. While the rash in this question is photosensitive, PCT is more commonly associated with sores or blisters on the hands, with the formation of milia as the blisters heal.

A. Dermatomyositis (DM)

While this rash does present in a similar way to the 'shawl sign' of DM, the absence of other symptoms makes this significantly less likely. With DM, one would expect periorbital oedema, metacarpophalangeal (MCP) papules or systemic symptoms such as significant unintentional weight loss or night sweats. The weight loss in this history is suggested to be intentional.

D. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

SLE is a multi-system disorder featuring a wide range of symptoms, including photosensitive rash. However, to reach a diagnosis, one would expect more systemic symptoms, including arthralgia, mouth ulcers or renal impairment. Drugs can induce SLE, including hydralazine, quinidine, isoniazid, minocycline and methyldopa; therefore, a thorough drug history is essential in these patients. The medications being taken by this patient are not likely to cause SLE.

E. Warfarin-induced photosensitivity

It is likely here that this is drug-induced photosensitivity. Therefore, the challenge is to identify the most likely offending drug. While it is theoretically possible for warfarin to cause photosensitivity, it is much more likely to be linked to antibiotics, such as doxycycline, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) or diuretics.

Therefore, this is not the correct answer.

questions.question: An 18-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a 3-week history of a rash across his trunk. He is otherwise well and denies any associated pain, itching or fever. Recently, he had a mild cough and cold that resolved spontaneously. There is no past medical history of note and he does not take any regular medications. His rash is examined and is shown below: What is the recommended management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
C. Reassurance and discharge

This patient has a diagnosis of pityriasis rosea, a self-limiting rash that characteristically develops after the appearance of a single pink/red patch called a herald patch. The rash then proceeds to spread in a fir-tree pattern, typically over the trunk. Viral symptoms can occur before the onset of the rash, but often patients can be asymptomatic and are generally well. In most cases, treatment is unnecessary as the rash will self-resolve after 2-3 months. In certain instances, patients may experience significant itching, in which case antihistamines, topical emollients or corticosteroids may be needed. In this case, treatment is not indicated due to this patient's absence of symptoms.

D. Topical betamethasone 0.1%

Topical betamethasone is a potent corticosteroid used in the management of significant eczema or psoriasis.

Although corticosteroids can be used in the management of pityriasis rosea in cases of significant itch, betamethasone is not the first-line choice. If corticosteroids are required, topical hydrocortisone would be preferred due to its lower potency and reduced risk of side-effects.

A. PO aciclovir

PO aciclovir is indicated for viral illnesses, particularly those caused by herpes simplex or varicella-zoster virus.

However, these rashes tend to have a vesicular appearance, which is not demonstrated here. Aciclovir does not play a role in the management of pityriasis rosea.

B. PO prednisolone

PO prednisolone can be used to treat some rashes, including lichen planus, an itchy rash that appears as flat- topped plaques. However, it is not used in the management of pityriasis rosea.

E. Topical ketoconazole

Topical ketoconazole is used in the management of pityriasis versicolor, a fungal skin infection caused by the yeast Malassezia furfur, which is commonly found as a skin-colonising organism. Pityriasis versicolor presents with either hypo- or hyperpigmented patches on the skin, with associated fine scale. The condition is also associated with hot weather, with triggers including a recent holiday to a warm destination.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman with sarcoidosis is admitted to hospital with diarrhoea. She has been previously fit and well and her sarcoid has been stable. Currently, she is under the care of the Dermatology Department for the management of a painful rash on her left leg. An image of the rash is seen below: While an in-patient, the diarrhoea clears up and the stool cultures return negative. She recalls that the Dermatologists commenced her on medication for the painful rash but cannot remember its name and she didn't bring the tablets with her to hospital. What is the most likely medication commenced by the Dermatology Department?
questions.explanation:
A. Colchicine

Colchicine is occasionally used for the treatment of erythema nodosum where it is particularly painful or disfiguring. It is the only one of the options to cause significant diarrhoea, making it the most likely answer here.

Other causes of erythema nodosum include streptococcal infection, tuberculosis, Salmonella, Campylobacter, histoplasmosis, ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, sulphonamides, Behçet's disease and pregnancy.

Image Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Heraldpatch2.jpg Medicalpal, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

C. Aspirin

Aspirin is not used as a treatment for erythema nodosum or in the treatment of sarcoidosis, it is therefore not the correct answer here.

B. Prednisolone

Although prednisolone is used for the treatment of sarcoidosis, it would not be expected to cause diarrhoea.

D. Dapsone

Dapsone is an alternative treatment for erythema nodosum but is not a prominent cause of diarrhoea.

E. Potassium iodide

This is used as a topical therapy for the treatment of erythema nodosum and would therefore not lead to any GI toxicity.

questions.question: A 56-year-old man is referred to the Dermatology Clinic by his General Practitioner (GP) with a recent history of weight loss and worsening constipation. Clinical examination is unremarkable, other than a rash in his axillae, and blood investigations which reveal a mild anaemia. Which one of the following test results is likely to be encountered?
options: A. Raised T3/T4 and low TSH
D. Raised levels of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)
E. Positive patch testing to common antiperspirant agents
questions.explanation:
D. Raised levels of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)

Acanthosis nigricans is linked with obesity and various endocrine disorders associated with insulin resistance such as diabetes, acromegaly and Cushing's syndrome. More rarely it is a paraneoplastic manifestation particularly of the gastrointestinal tract. The CEA test measures the amount of this protein in the serum and is often raised in people with certain kinds of cancers, especially cancer of the large intestine (colon and rectum).

A. Raised T3/T4 and low TSH

Acanthosis nigricans is a diffuse velvety thickening and hyperpigmentation of the skin. It occurs mainly in the axillae and other intertriginous areas. It is linked to various endocrine disorders including hypothyroidism, but not hyperthyroidism.

B. Positive direct immunofluorescence

Direct immunofluorescence is a technique that involves the application of fluorescent antibodies to samples of patient tissue obtained from biopsies, and is used in dermatological practice in order to confirm the diagnosis of suspected autoimmune bullous diseases, connective tissue diseases and vasculitides.

C. Low Vitamin D levels

Acanthosis nigricans is not linked to vitamin D deficiency.

E. Positive patch testing to common antiperspirant agents

Patch testing is used to help confirm the presence of contact allergic reactions. These typically cause itchy, dermatitic skin rashes and are unrelated to acanthosis nigricans.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman visits her General Practitioner (GP). She complains of localised hair loss in the vertex of her scalp, associated with itching irritation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Cicatricial alopecia

In cicatricial alopecia (also known as scarring alopecia) inflammation injures hair follicles resulting in permanent bald patches with no visible follicles. In this case the presence of inflammation can be seen as redness, scaling and crusting. Common causes for cicatricial alopecia include discoid lupus erythematosus, and lichen planopilaris (a variant of lichen planus). Treatment is dependent on the underlying causes but often requires topical corticosteroids. Given the fact some hair follicles have been destroyed and no regeneration is possible, treatment is aimed at reducing the amount of inflammation and minimising further hair loss

D. Trichotillomania

Trichotillomania describes a psychological disorder where patients are compelled to pull their own hair, resulting in alopecia. It is typically encountered in teenage females and children, leading to irregular patches of alopecia that are not commonly associated with a scarring process unless encountered in chronic, severe forms.

B. Alopecia areata

Alopecia areata (AA) is a condition characterised by recurrent non-scarring patches of hair loss that can affect any hair-bearing area of skin. In the areas affected, the skin is normal in appearance. In the periphery there may be short, broken hairs that taper at the proximal end (exclamation point hairs) - this is a pathognomonic sign but is not always present. Patients may also complain of pruritus or a burning sensation in the affected skin areas. AA can occur at any age and affects both sexes equally. The natural history of the condition is unpredictable with no correlation existing between the number of patches at onset and the subsequent severity of the disease. Precipitating factors can be found in some patients but not all patients, and include: stressful events, febrile illnesses, drugs and pregnancy.

C. Androgenetic alopecia

Androgenetic alopecia (also known as pattern hair loss) does not cause erythema, scale and crusting. It occurs due to genetic factors and hormonal influences. Androgenetic alopecia is apparent is about 50% of individual; by the age of 50 years. Typically, in men it affects the vertex and temporal scalp, whereas in women it is more diffuse and worst on the anterior scalp.

E. Telogen effluvium

Telogen effluvium is a diffuse, temporary, non-scarring form of alopecia where hair is lost 2-3 months following stressful events such as severe illnesses, accidents and childbirth. Telogen effluvium is self-limiting and requires no medical interventions.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman presents to her Primary Care Clinic with a complaint of painful sores at the corners of her mouth. The lesions have been persistent for several weeks and are associated with a mild burning sensation when she eats. She has a past medical history of irritable bowel syndrome but is otherwise healthy. On examination, erythematous cracks and fissures are observed bilaterally at the corners of her mouth. There is no lymphadenopathy, and the rest of her oral mucosa is unremarkable. She reports no recent weight loss or changes in diet.
InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)112 g/L135–175 g/L
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV)78 fL80–100 fL
Serum ferritin8 µg/L15–200 µg/L
Vitamin B12300 pg/mL200–900 pg/mL
Folate5 ng/mL2–20 ng/mL
What is the most likely underlying cause of this patient's angular stomatitis?
questions.explanation:
B. Iron deficiency

Iron deficiency is a common cause of angular stomatitis due to its role in maintaining the integrity of epithelial tissues. The patient's low Hb level, low MCV and low ferritin level indicate iron deficiency anaemia, which is likely contributing to her symptoms.

C. Vitamin C deficiency

Vitamin C deficiency can cause oral symptoms, such as bleeding gums and poor wound healing, but it is less commonly associated with angular stomatitis. There are no other signs of scurvy (eg bleeding gums, petechiae) in this patient, making it an unlikely cause.

A. Vitamin B12 deficiency

Vitamin B12 deficiency may cause angular stomatitis in severe cases, along with other oral manifestations such as glossitis. However, this patient's vitamin B12 level is within the normal range, making this an unlikely cause.

D. Herpes simplex virus infection

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection typically presents with painful vesicular lesions rather than with chronic fissures at the mouth corners. HSV lesions are also usually recurrent and present with clusters of vesicles, which are not seen in this patient's presentation.

E. Fungal infection

Fungal infections, especially those with Candida species, can lead to angular stomatitis. However, candidal infections are more commonly seen in immunocompromised patients or those with poor oral hygiene or dentures. This patient's low Hb and ferritin levels suggest an underlying nutritional deficiency rather than an infectious cause.

questions.question: A 57-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with hair loss, distributed on the front and crown of her scalp but sparing the sides. She denied using braids, straighteners, tongs or wearing a ponytail. She had no other significant medical problems. What is the most appropriate initial intervention to treat her hair loss?
questions.explanation:
A. Topical Minoxidil

This patient has hair loss in a pattern either related to androgen excess or to increased sensitivity to androgens.

Topical treatment of choice is minoxidil, which promotes hair re-growth. Other options include systemic anti- androgens such as finasteride.

B. Oral Minoxidil

Oral minoxidil is a vasodilator used for resistant hypertension, and it was found in clinical trials to stimulate hair growth as a side-effect of therapy.

C. Laser therapy

Laser therapy is of course used for hair removal rather than to stimulate hair growth.

D. Topical steroids

Topical steroids are used in scarring alopecia to reduce inflammation.

E. Antifungal shampoo

Anti-fungal shampoo is used to treat seborrheic dermatitis and pityriasis versicolor.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man with no previous cardiovascular events presents for evaluation of persistently elevated cholesterol levels. He reports a family history of heart disease, with his father suffering a myocardial infarction at the age of 50 years. On examination, there are xanthomas on his elbows and Achilles tendons. His lipid profile reveals a total cholesterol level of 9.0 mmol/l and a low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol level of 7.5 mmol/l. Genetic testing confirms a diagnosis of heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH). What is the most appropriate management plan for this patient?
options: A. Lifestyle changes alone, with dietary counselling
B. Initiate a high-intensity statin and consider adding ezetimibe if LDL cholesterol target levels are not met
D. Prescribe a bile acid sequestrant as monotherapy
E. Start a fibrate and monitor lipid levels after six months
questions.explanation:
B. Initiate a high-intensity statin and consider adding ezetimibe if LDL cholesterol target levels are not

met This is the correct answer. High-intensity statins, such as atorvastatin or rosuvastatin, are first-line agents for significantly lowering LDL cholesterol levels in patients with FH. If LDL cholesterol target levels are not reached, ezetimibe can be added to achieve further reduction. This approach aligns with current guidelines for managing FH to lower cardiovascular risk.

E. Start a fibrate and monitor lipid levels after six months

Fibrates primarily reduce triglyceride levels and have a limited effect on LDL cholesterol levels. They are not typically used as first-line therapy for FH where aggressive LDL cholesterol reduction is essential. Statins are preferred for achieving significant LDL cholesterol reductions.

A. Lifestyle changes alone, with dietary counselling

While lifestyle modifications and dietary counselling are important supportive measures, they are insufficient for FH. Due to the genetic nature of FH and markedly elevated LDL cholesterol levels, pharmacological intervention is necessary to achieve significant reductions.

C. Start inclisiran

Inclisiran, a small interfering RNA therapy, reduces LDL cholesterol levels by inhibiting PCSK9 production. It is approved for use in primary hypercholesterolaemia and as adjunctive therapy in FH when statin therapy alone does not achieve LDL cholesterol target levels. However, it is generally added only if patients do not achieve LDL cholesterol target levels with a statin and ezetimibe combination.

D. Prescribe a bile acid sequestrant as monotherapy

Bile acid sequestrants can be used as an adjunct to statin therapy but are not recommended as monotherapy for FH, given their limited LDL cholesterol-lowering capacity and the risk of GI side-effects. Statins remain the mainstay of treatment.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with a one week history of painful mouth ulcers and blistering lesions over the face and upper body. He also complains of some general malaise. On examination, he has evidence of gingival erosions and bullae over the scalp and chest. The lesionsare friable, and some have crusted over. A Nikolsky sign is positive. What is the most likely cause of the presentation?
questions.explanation:
D. Pemphigus vulgaris (PV)

The answer is Pemphigus vulgaris (PV) (Option D).

PV is an autoimmune intra-epithelial, blistering disease, affecting the skin and mucous membranes, that is mediated by circulating autoantibodies directed against keratinocyte cell surfaces. It can present with erosions in the mouth and flaccid blisters on the skin. The cause of PV remains unknown, but there is a recognised association with the human leukocyte antigen DR4 (DRB1*0402) and human leukocyte antigen DRw6 (DQB1*0503) alleles. Patients often also have other autoimmune diseases, particularly myasthenia gravis and thymoma.

E. Bullous impetigo

Bullous impetigo (Option E) is incorrect.

This uncommon form of impetigo presents with small vesicles that evolve into flaccid, transparent bullae. It is due to staphylococcal exfoliative toxins, which target desmoglein 1 and cleave off the superficial epidermis.

A. Erythema multiforme

Erythema multiforme (Option A) is incorrect.

The typical target lesions of erythema multiforme have a sharp margin, a round shape and three concentric zones of colours (and possibly a blister in the middle). Erythema multiforme may involve the mouth with multiple irregular erosions. Extensive involvement of the mouth, lips, conjunctivae and genitalia is called Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Infections are probably associated with at least 90% of cases of erythema multiforme, with the most common infections being herpes simplex virus and Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

Management is supportive.

B. Bullous pemphigoid

Bullous pemphigoid (Option B) is incorrect.

This is an immune-mediated blistering disorder that presents with tense blisters in the elderly. It uncommonly affects the mucosae and may be preceded by an itchy rash lasting from days to weeks (pre-bullous pemphigoid).

C. Dermatitis herpetiformis

Dermatitis herpetiformis (Option C) is incorrect.

Dermatitis herpetiformis occurs in close association with coeliac disease and presents with very itchy, grouped vesicles, most frequent on the extensor surface of the knees, elbows, buttocks and shoulders. Treatment is with dapsone and a gluten-free diet.

questions.question: A 47-year-old obese woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) complaining of an erythematous rash affecting her groin. She has a history of Type II diabetes for which she takes Metformin and follows a diabetic diet, but is otherwise relatively well. On examination, her blood pressure (BP) is 152/88 mmHg. Her pulse is 80 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. There is an erythematous rash affecting the skin creases on both sides of her groin and the upper inside aspect of both thighs. Skin scrapings reveal S. epidermidis and T. rubrum. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
questions.explanation:
E. Topical Ketoconazole

The answer is Topical Ketoconazole - Tinea cruris as a result of Trichophyton rubrum infection is the most likely cause of this patient's groin rash. In the first instance topical azole antifungal therapy is sufficient to clear infection for the majority of patients. As such topical Ketoconazole is the most appropriate initial intervention here.

A. IV Flucloxacillin

IV Flucloxacillin is incorrect because the S. epidermidis growth here is likely to represent normal skin flora rather than the cause of her rash.

B. Oral Flucloxacillin

Oral Flucloxacillin, is incorrect because the S. epidermidis growth here is likely to represent normal skin flora rather than the cause of her rash.

C. Oral Griseofulvin

Oral Griseofulvin, is incorrect because Griseofulvin inhibits fungal cell division, rather than being a fungicidal agent, as such a more prolonged course is usually required versus azole therapies. It is also associated with hepatic dysfunction and is a potent p450 inducer.

D. Oral Itraconazole

Oral Itraconazole, is incorrect, this is a potential option for patients whose infection fails to clear in response to topical therapy alone. 40418

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman attends the General Practice (GP) Surgery with a long history of recurrent red marks on her torso. These slowly expand by two to three mm per day into annular shapes that clear centrally, and then fade over days to weeks, leaving normal skin. Some of the lesions have fine scaling in their inner erythematous rim. They can reach a maximum of 10 cm in diameter. They have a seasonal preponderance, appearing every summer. She is otherwise well. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
D. Erythema annulare centrifugum

EAC is an idiopathic, chronic, recurrent erythema, which is often seasonal. Triggers can be drugs or infections.

Topical steroids usually cause involution of the treated lesions, but they do not prevent the occurrence of new lesions or recurrence of lesions at the original site.

E. Erythema gyratum repens

Erythema gyratum repens is a paraneoplastic skin rash consisting of urticated, wavy erythematous bands like 'grains of wood' most often associated with carcinoma of the lung. These expand quickly at a rate of up to 1 cm/day.

A. Erythema marginatum

Erythema marginatum is characterised by macules that spread into patches associated with acute rheumatic fever (fever, carditis, migratory polyarthritis) caused by group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal infection.

B. Erythema migrans

Erythema migrans develops 7 days after a tick bite and is a sign of Lyme disease. Lesions range from 10-50 cm in diameter and flu-like symptoms are common. Lyme serology is a key investigation when this is identified.

C. Erythema induratum

Erythema induratum of Bazin is a nodular vasculitis (tender erythematous, indurated nodules and plaques), especially on the lower legs, associated with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Further investigations including chest X-ray and sputum culture are recommended when this is identified.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a one week history of cellulitis of the middle finger of her left hand. This has occurred twice before in the last year and resolved after two to three weeks. On each occasion, she presented with cellulitis and painful lymphadenopathy of the left axilla, and was treated with intravenous (IV) antibiotics. Wound swabs, blood cultures and fungal cultures were negative. On examination, the patient had a vesiculo-pustular plaque on the distal phalanx, with lesions on the ulnar border of the middle phalanx. There was ascending lymphangitis on the dorsum of the left hand extending proximally to the mid-forearm, and painful lymphadenopathy. Prolonged tissue culture for acid-fast bacilli is sent. An X-ray of the left finger shows no bony abnormality. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the left hand shows high signal within the soft tissue of the middle finger consistent with oedema. What is the most appropriate management option in this case?
options: A. Aciclovir 400 mg 5 times a day
C. Benzyl penicillin 1.2 g qds + flucloxacillin 1 g intravenously qds
questions.explanation:
A. Aciclovir 400 mg 5 times a day

The clinical features and recurrent nature at the same site are diagnostic for Herpes simplex infection, known on a digit as herpetic whitlow. This may cause secondary cellulitis, lymphangitis and lymphadenitis. Rarely, lymphoedema may follow. The diagnosis should be confirmed on a viral swab, usually via culture or polymerase chain reaction test. Uncomplicated disease may not require treatment, but given the complications in the scenario, aciclovir should be commenced (maximum- 2 gm per day). In recurrent disease, prophylaxis (aciclovir 400 mg bd) is appropriate.

B. Anti-tuberculous therapy

Cutaneous lesions of tuberculosis would not be episodic and the appearance in the photograph is characteristic of Herpes simplex infection.

C. Benzyl penicillin 1.2 g qds + flucloxacillin 1 g intravenously qds

This might be appropriate for super-added bacterial infection, but the symptoms and signs are fully compatible with Herpes simplex infection.

D. Prednisolone 60 mg od

This would risk worsening Herpes simplex infection, the diagnosis of which is clear from the photograph.

E. Surgical debridement

This has no place in the management of herpetic whitlow, the diagnosis of which is clear from the photograph.

questions.question: A 36-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with a widespread rash. He has been feeling unwell and has a poor appetite. On examination, he is found to have an erythematous rash with areas of blistering, shown below. His lips are eroded, and multiple aphthous ulcers are noticed in the mouth. The eyes are injected. What is the most appropriate management option for the oral ulcers?
questions.explanation:
A. Chlorhexidine mouthwash

The answer is Chlorhexidine mouthwash (Option A).

This patient has Stevens-Johnson syndrome and may require hospital admission for nutritional support and adequate skin care. The causes of Stevens-Johnson syndrome are as for erythema multiforme, but with drugs, rather than infections, being the most common culprit. It is therefore imperative to stop any recently started medications. Management is supportive. Use of chlorhexidine mouthwash may be helpful in preventing secondary infections.

C. Intravenous (IV) flucloxacillin

Intravenous (IV) flucloxacillin (Option C) is incorrect.

Antibiotics are not useful in Steven-Johnson syndrome, unless used to treat secondary bacterial infections.

Throat swabs for the detection of Streptococcus and chest X-rays looking for evidence of Mycoplasma pneumoniae may be of use.

B. Topical steroids

Topical steroids (Option B) is incorrect.

There is no evidence that topical steroids are helpful in achieving faster resolution of the erosions and rash.

D. IV immunoglobulins

IV immunoglobulins (Option D) is incorrect.

IV immunoglobulins should be considered in the management of toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). In Stevens- Johnson syndrome, supportive care and cessation of the offending agents form the mainstay of care.

E. Azathioprine

Azathioprine (Option E) is incorrect.

This is a steroid-sparing agent used in the long-term management of a number of skin disorders such as eczema, cutaneous vasculitis, cutaneous systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), bullous pemphigoid and pemphigus vulgaris. 33389

questions.question: A 40-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with reddish skin lesions on the tongue, cheeks and nose for the past year. He gives a past history of frequent moderate to severe nasal bleeding since childhood. He had received a blood transfusion twice for correction of his anaemia. On further enquiry, he states that he has had two episodes of black, tarry stools over the past three months. A picture of his facial lesions is shown below: Which of the following is characteristic of this patient's condition?
options: D. Recurrent epistaxis due to platelet dysfunction
E. Recurrent gastrointestinal haemorrhage due to increased predisposition to peptic ulcer disease
questions.explanation:
C. Multiple mucocutaneous telangiectasia

Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, with variable penetrance and expression. Telangiectasia of the skin and buccal mucosa are seen in the majority of individuals with HHT in later life. They mostly occur on the lips, tongue, buccal mucosa and fingertips.

Image credit: CC BY 2.5 https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HereditaryHemorrhagicTelangiectasia.jpg

B. Autosomal recessive inheritance

The inheritance pattern for HHT is autosomal dominant, so autosomal recessive inheritance is not appropriate here.

A. An unremarkable family history

The three major disease-associated genes include ENG, ACVRL1 and SMAD4. The presence of the disease in a first-degree relative is one of the diagnostic criteria. Hence, an unremarkable family history is not characteristic of this disease.

D. Recurrent epistaxis due to platelet dysfunction

The skin lesions in this patient are indicative of abnormal dilated capillaries on the tongue, cheeks and nose.

The skin lesions, along with the clinical presentation, make the diagnosis of HHT likely. The most common clinical manifestation of HHT is spontaneous, recurrent epistaxis from a telangiectatic lesion in the nasal mucosa. Epistaxis does not occur due to platelet dysfunction in these patients.

E. Recurrent gastrointestinal haemorrhage due to increased predisposition to peptic ulcer disease

Arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) can occur in a number of organs such as the lung, brain and liver.

Cerebrovascular accidents and transient ischaemic attacks occur in patients with AVMs in the brain and can result in significant morbidity and mortality. Hence, it is much more likely for this patient to have recurrent gastrointestinal haemorrhage from visceral AVMs, rather than from peptic ulcer disease.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with an enlarging rash over his shin, which was associated with significant swelling and discomfort. Four days earlier, he had undergone a surgical procedure to his varicose veins. On examination, he is sweaty and anxious. He has a low-grade fever and tachycardia of 130 beats per minute (bpm). His blood pressure (BP) is 120/80 mmHg. There is an extensive brownish red discoloration over the whole shin and significant associated swelling. There is also a crackly sensation when the swollen area is palpated, and a pungent discharge from an open site at the distal end of the affected area. What is the most important treatment option?
questions.explanation:
B. Surgical debridement

The answer is Surgical debridement (Option B).

Gas gangrene is a medical emergency. It is caused, in the vast majority of cases, by Clostridium perfringens infection, and the clinical presentation fits best with this diagnosis. Rapid onset of muscle necrosis, gas production and sepsis are the hallmarks of this disease. C. perfringens is an exotoxin-producing clostridial species (large, Gram-positive, spore-forming bacillus), which is normally found in soil and the gastrointestinal tract.

The most common clinical presentation is with post-traumatic gas gangrene, which occurs through direct inoculation of contaminated ischaemic wounds.

Spontaneous gas gangrene may be caused through the haematogenous spread of toxin-producing bacteria (often in patients who are immunocompromised or those with diabetes).

Immediate management involves resuscitation with oxygen and intravenous fluids to stabilise the patient.

Surgical debridement is the definitive treatment.

E. IV immunoglobulin

IV immunoglobulins (Option E) is incorrect.

Immunoglobulin therapy is used in a wide variety of conditions such as immune-mediated thrombocytopenia and Guillain-Barré syndrome. Some evidence is available that supports its use in severe sepsis as an add-on treatment.

A. Hyperbaric oxygen

Hyperbaric oxygen (Option A) is incorrect.

This is used in multiple situations such as decompression sickness, air emboli and the healing of chronic wounds. It is also used against severe soft tissue infections, like gas gangrene and necrotising fasciitis, but its role is supportive.

C. Intravenous (IV) penicillin

Intravenous (IV) penicillin (Option C) is incorrect.

Certain antibiotics (including penicillin) alone are not effective enough treatment because they cannot penetrate the affected tissues sufficiently enough to be effective.

D. Tetanus toxoid

Tetanus toxoid (Option D) is incorrect.

Tetanus toxoid is a vaccine given in childhood for the prevention of tetanus. In immune patients, additional tetanus toxoid can be given in adulthood to booster immunity following high-risk injuries. In non-immunised individuals with high-risk injuries, tetanus antitoxin may also be administered.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She has an intensely itchy rash with vesicles and blisters, which she says waxes and wanes from week to week. She has suffered from irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) symptoms in the past and her anti-Tissue Transglutaminase (anti-TTG) antibodies are positive. Despite following a gluten-free diet and being prescribed dapsone, she is still suffering from the rash. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
E. Oral sulfapyridine

Although following a gluten-free diet ±dapsone does improve the rash of dermatitis herpetiformis significantly in many patients, some still suffer resistant symptoms. In those adult patients, sulfapyridine may be given at a starting dose of 0.5 g three times per day, which may be increased to up to 6 g per day if necessary to control patient symptoms. Risks of therapy include agranulocytosis and hypersensitivity.

A. Oral azathioprine

Although some patients gain a response to azathioprine, it is less effective vs dapsone and sulfa-based compounds.

B. Oral methotrexate

Methotrexate isn't used for the treatment of dermatitis herpetiformis; in rare cases it is recognised to cause a coeliac disease-like syndrome with a dermatitis herpetiformis-type rash.

C. Oral prednisolone

Oral steroids should be avoided in the treatment of dermatitis herpetiformis if possible because of the benefit risk profile associated with systemic therapy.

D. Topical high-potency steroids

Topical high-potency steroids are an alternative to sulfapyridine, but given the often extensive nature of the rash, cumulative systemic absorption of steroids may be quite high.

questions.question: A 61-year-old woman with end-stage kidney disease presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a six week history of progressive, painful tightening of the skin leading to disabling joint contractures. She denies having any difficulty swallowing, but admits to progressively worsening shortness of breath since the onset of her symptoms. She also complains of severe bone pain. She had a contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan two months earlier to rule out a slipped disc. On examination, she has symmetrically distributed, indurated, woody plaques on the trunk and lower limbs. Her face, neck and nails are normal. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
E. Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis

Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is a devastating cutaneous dermopathy seen in patients with end-stage kidney disease, and who have been exposed to gadolinium-based contrast agents seen in MRI. Metformin may also be a potential trigger, although the exact pathophysiological mechanism for the condition is unknown.

Complications include pulmonary fibrosis, cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension.

A. Systemic sclerosis

In systemic sclerosis a more prolonged course of symptoms would be expected, with other features such as Raynaud's, telangiectasia and nail changes not seen here.

B. Plaque morphoea

Morphea is usually asymptomatic, with asymmetrical areas of cutaneous fibrosis consistent with scleroderma developing over a period of many months, without the proximity, as here to gadolinium contrast material.

C. Scleromyxoedema

Scleromyxoedema is a rare progressive cutaneous mucinosis associated with progressive deposition of mucin within connective tissue, and often a paraproteinaemia.

D. Pre-tibia myxoedema

Pre-tibial myxoedema is confined to the shins and is associated with oedema and fibrosis, and with thyroid dysfunction.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman came to the General Practitioner with complaints of pruritic skin lesions for the past three years. She was previously treated with terbinafine cream, without any resolution. She was on aceclofenac for chronic low back pain. A skin biopsy is done and histopathological examination showed focal parakeratosis and superficial and deep perivascular mononuclear infiltrate, with characteristic cuffing in a coat sleeve fashion. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
A. Erythema annular centrifugum

The lesion characteristics, age, medication history (history of aceclofenac intake) and the histopathological findings indicate a diagnosis of erythema annular centrifugum. The lesion characteristics in this patient may be described as thick, red, scaly lesions on both arms, thighs and buttocks. The lesions show central clearing with erythematous raised edges. This is characteristic of the diagnosis of erythema annular centrifugum.

Image credit: CC BY 4.0, Victor Desmond Mandel, Barbara Ferrari, Marco Manfredini, Francesca Giusti and Giovanni Pellacani https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Erythema_annulare_centrifugum_on_arms_and_legs.jpg

C. Erythema marginatum

This patient has no features of rheumatic fever such as fever, painful and tender joints, chest pain, shortness of breath and fatigue. This makes the diagnosis of erythema marginatum unlikely.

B. Erythema migrans

Erythema migrans is seen in Lyme's disease. However, the absence of a history of fever, fatigue, arthralgia or lymphadenopathy makes this diagnosis unlikely.

D. Erythema gyratum repens

In erythema gyratum repens, the lesions tend to migrate at a rapid speed (1 cm/day). Since this patient has no such history, erythema gyratum repens would not be appropriate. In addition, underlying lung, breast and gastrointestinal cancers may be detected.

E. Tinea corporis

Plaques of tinea corporis tend to have more scaling and pruritus is more severe. In addition, the lesions did not respond to terbinafine make the diagnosis of tinea corporis unlikely.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with bilateral itchy legs, which he has found increasingly difficult to manage over the past two to three months. He has a background of kidney disease, secondary to type II diabetes mellitus, and is undergoing haemodialysis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Xerosis

'Xerosis' simply means dry skin and is a common complication of uraemia secondary to chronic kidney disease and dialysis. Uraemic patients commonly suffer from pruritus.

D. Pre-tibial myxoedema

Pre-tibial myxoedema, or Graves' dermopathy, is an infiltrative dermopathy resulting in a peau d'orange appearance and non-pitting oedema.

B. Lipodermatosclerosis

Lipodermatosclerosis is often associated with pain and causes tapering of the skin above the ankles, forming a constricting band resembling an inverted champagne bottle. There may be redness, induration and pigmentation.

C. Lichen simplex chronicus

Lichen simplex chronicus is caused by an itch-scratch cycle which starts after an underlying pruritic skin complaint such as eczema, irritant or allergic dermatitis or psoriasis. It looks like distinct patches of thick, brown leathery skin.

E. Scurvy

Scurvy results in purpura or ecchymoses (bruises) and corkscrew hairs rather than the picture of dry scaling skin seen here.

questions.question: A 47-year-old man is referred to the Dermatology Clinic with a one year history of a lesion developing on the left upper lip, which has steadily enlarged. There is no history of itching or bleeding. He was noted to be a keen user of sun beds. The lesion is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Basal cell carcinoma (BCC)

The image shows a nodular lesion below the left nasolabial fold with telangectasia. The most likely diagnosis is that of a BCC. This is the most common non-melanoma skin malignancy. BCCs (or rodent ulcers) most commonly occur in middle-aged or elderly fair-skinned individuals with significant sun exposure. Most occur on the face but can also occur on the limbs and trunk. BCCs usually start as a small, translucent papule with telangiectasia over the surface. They gradually increase in size, developing into firm, tethered nodules, with a centre that may ulcerate and crust. The most common treatment is with surgical excision or radiotherapy.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Basal-cell_Carcinoma.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Basal-cell_Carcinoma.jpg) - This file is licensed under the Creative Commons (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/en:Creative_Commons) Attribution-Share Alike 4.0 International (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/deed.en) license.

C. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)

Cutaneous SCC is the second most common types of non-melanoma skin cancer. They present as enlarging scaly or crusted lumps which often arise within pre-existing actinic keratoses or areas of Bowen's disease.

A. Nodular melanoma

A. malignant melanoma is a tumour of the melanocytes. Two-thirds arise from normal skin, and one-third from

pre-existing moles. Even though commonly encountered, melanomas are more rare than non-melanoma skin cancers. It is important to diagnose and treat melanomas while they are thin, so that removal may result in favourable prognostic outcomes.

D. Atypical fibroxanthoma (AFX)

An AFX is an uncommon type of skin cancer, accounting for < 0.2% of all skin cancers. It occurs mainly on the head or neck of older people with significant sun exposure. Typically, AFX is a red, juicy, dome-shaped nodule that may be bleeding, ulcerated or crusted.

E. Pyogenic granuloma

Pyogenic granuloma is a benign growth of blood vessels. It presents as a growing fleshy lump, which may bleed easily. It is often the product of physical trauma, infection or hormonal changes such as pregnancy.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman is reviewed in the Outpatient Clinic. A picture of the patient's finger nails is shown below: Which of the following conditions are they most likely to suffer from?
