Systemic therapy may include antibiotics, cautious use of systemic corticosteroids, and treatment with anti-inflammatory agents such as methotrexate or biologicals.

C. Start oral corticosteroids

Systemic corticosteroids are should only be used with high levels of caution in pustular psoriasis due to the high risk of rebound after completion of treatment. It can be considered as a treatment, but this should be done with monitoring as an inpatient.

B. Refer for ultraviolet (UV) light therapy

UV treatment is appropriate in plaque psoriasis and also in palmoplantar psoriasis. However, it is not appropriate treatment in pustular psoriasis.

D. Arrange for outpatient intravenous (IV) antibiotics

This could be appropriate for patients with severe cellulitis who are systemically well. This patient does not have cellulitis, and the ongoing systemic symptoms and rapidly evolving nature of his symptoms means that he would not be suitable for this therapy.

E. Start topical treatment with potent corticosteroids and vitamin D

This would be first-line treatment for plaque psoriasis and is not appropriate for pustular psoriasis. 71631

questions.question: A 23-year-old man presents to the General Medical Clinic with a new, itchy rash. He has no previous medical problems. He has not had any previous skin problems. He denies any intravenous (IV) drug abuse. A photograph of his skin is shown below: What is the most appropriate management plan?
questions.explanation:
A. Topical ketoconazole

This patient has a typical rash of tinea corporis. Tinea corporis, commonly known as ringworm, is a dermatophyte fungal infection of the trunk, legs or arms. Different species cause this infection depending on the part of the world the patient is in. Clinically, there may be an acute or chronic rash, spreading from the infected site. The rash is characterised by itchy, inflamed red patches which may be pustular, an oval shape. There are characteristic rings as the rash spreads. Treatment should be with topical antifungal agents in the first instance, and if there is treatment failure then oral antifungal treatment can be considered.

D. Topical vitamin D

Topical vitamin D is used in conjunction with topical corticosteroids for psoriasis. Psoriasis typically presents as plaques of silvery scales on top of a salmon-pink rash.

B. Oral terbinafine

Oral antifungal treatment would be effective, but generally topical treatment should be first-line. Terbinafine and other antifungals can cause liver injury, as well as gastrointestinal upset.

C. Topical corticosteroids

The pattern of this patient's rash is consistent with a fungal infection. Steroid treatment would cause immunosuppression and make the infection worse, causing further spread. Had this been a condition such as eczema or psoriasis, then corticosteroids would have been appropriate. The key differentiating factor is the spreading element of the rash, the ring-like appearance and the location.

E. Refer to oncology

This would have been appropriate for patients with a malignant melanoma. Melanomas are typically pigmented lesions characterised by irregular edge, change in colour, symptoms of bleeding, itching and sensation, as well as ongoing change. In such patients, an urgent two-week referral is warranted.

questions.question: A 19-year-old woman with a history of severe facial acne resistant to treatment with topical therapies and systemic antibiotics comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She has no history of previous psychiatric illness, has read about isotretinoin and would like to start therapy. She is not currently sexually active. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Advise that the medication is not appropriate for someone of her age
B. Beta human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) one month pre-therapy and initiate contraception
D. Initiate therapy and advise her to use contraception if she becomes sexually active
E. Initiate therapy and advise a pregnancy test if she becomes sexually active
questions.explanation:
B. Beta human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) one month pre-therapy and initiate contraception

Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen, hence pregnancy must be absolutely avoided in women who are taking it. The medicine is considered contraindicated, unless the terms of a pregnancy prevention programme are met. The fact that she is currently abstinent does not exempt her from this.

E. Initiate therapy and advise a pregnancy test if she becomes sexually active

This option could still potentially expose the fetus to a potent teratogen if she becomes pregnant while on the medication.

A. Advise that the medication is not appropriate for someone of her age

Severe facial acne which has failed to respond to topical therapies and systemic antibiotics is an indication for isotretinoin. However, given it is a potent teratogen, it is imperative that patients adhere to contraceptive methods.

C. Initiate therapy and contraception

It is important for a patient to have a negative pregnancy test and then to have a full month on contraception one month before the initiation of therapy.

D. Initiate therapy and advise her to use contraception if she becomes sexually active

This option could still potentially expose the fetus to a potent teratogen if she was already pregnant at the time of initiating therapy.

questions.question: A 21-year-old man presents to the clinic with complaints of a tingling sensation over the lower limbs and seizures for the past year. He gives a history of decreased visual acuity and photophobia since childhood. He also has a history of recurrent respiratory infections and easy bruising following minor trauma. On examination, there are multiple patches of depigmentation over the face, trunk and limbs, and silvery hair was seen. A peripheral smear reveals an accumulation of large granules in neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Chediak-Higashi syndrome

The diagnosis of Chediak-Higashi syndrome is supported by the presence of oculocutaneous albinism, a history of bleeding diathesis, recurrent infections, peripheral neuropathy and the presence of giant granules on leukocytes.

E. Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome

Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome presents with oculocutaneous albinism, pulmonary fibrosis and bleeding diathesis, but with no silvery hair, neurological involvement and giant granules.

A. Angelman syndrome

Angelman syndrome usually presents during childhood with craniofacial abnormalities, feeding problems, developmental delay and hypogonadism.

C. Elejalde syndrome

Elejalde syndrome presents with silvery hair, depigmentation with bronze tan on sun exposure and a lack of immunological dysfunction.

D. Griscelli syndrome

Griscelli syndrome shows severe neurological involvement and immunological dysfunction, along with silvery hair, but without giant granules.

questions.question: A 16-year-old girl presents to the Dermatology Clinic with an itchy rash across her body. She has no history of allergies and has never had a rash like this before. Approximately two weeks ago, she required a course of antibiotics for a sore throat. She is usually fit and well and helps in a children's nursery. Her rash is examined, as shown below: Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
A. Narrowband UVB phototherapy

This patient has a likely diagnosis of guttate psoriasis, given the history of an acute-onset itchy rash that has the appearance of multiple erythematous plaques with silver scale. Often, the lesions can have a teardrop shape to them. Guttate psoriasis is a subtype of psoriasis and can be triggered by a recent streptococcal infection. The patient's history of a recent sore throat requiring antibiotics is a risk factor for guttate psoriasis.

Guttate psoriasis responds well to phototherapy, which is often given in acute management of the condition. In contrast, phototherapy is often used later in the management of chronic plaque-type psoriasis.

B. PO acitretin

Acitretin is a systemic retinoid that helps to regulate epithelial cell growth. However, it is a third-line agent that is reserved for those who fail to respond to other treatments. Additionally, retinoids should be prescribed with caution in women of childbearing age - this would need to be taken into consideration for this patient.

C. PO ciclosporin

PO ciclosporin is a disease-modifying agent used as a second-line treatment for psoriasis. It is a potent immunosuppressive agent and generally has good action against psoriasis. Therefore, ciclosporin is generally reserved for emergency presentations, including erythroderma. However, it has considerable side-effects such as nephrotoxicity.

D. PO methotrexate

PO methotrexate is another disease-modifying agent used in the management of psoriasis. It is a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor that works as an antiproliferative and anti-inflammatory agent. It is often used as a systemic drug of choice in patients with psoriasis and evidence of psoriatic arthropathy. Similarly to ciclosporin, methotrexate should be used with caution in women of childbearing age.

E. Topical hydrocortisone

Topical corticosteroids are frequently used either alone or in combination with vitamin D analogues (eg Dovobet ®) in the management of psoriasis, particularly chronic plaque-type psoriasis. Although topical corticosteroids (along with other topical agents such as salicylic acid and coal tar) are common first-line measures to treat psoriasis, guttate psoriasis responds better to light therapy.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman, who is 34 weeks pregnant, presents to the Dermatology Clinic with an erythematous, blistering rash on her upper thigh and abdomen. She has no history of systemic illness and the pregnancy has been unremarkable so far. She has no past medical history of note and took no regular medication before her pregnancy. On examination, there are multiple small, irregularly shaped blisters over the lower abdomen and the tops of her thighs. Her blood pressure (BP) and temperature are normal.

InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)109 g/L115–155 g/L

Given the likely dermatological diagnosis, which of the following represents the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
questions.explanation:
C. Corticosteroid ointment

The presenting case is consistent with Pemphigoid gestationis (PG), which is a bullous autoimmune, sub- epidermal dermatosis clinically and pathogenetically similar to bullous pemphigoid. It occurs during the third trimester and less commonly in the second trimester or even after delivery. High-potency topical corticosteroids are indicated for localised disease, e.g. her lower abdomen and top of thighs.

B. Acyclovir ointment

This condition is not viral in nature and therefore will not respond to acyclovir.

A. Oral prednisolone

This treatment line is indicated if topical steroids are not controlling the symptoms.

D. Oral antihistamines

This may only help with symptomatic pruritus control rather than treating the autoimmune condition.

E. Intravenous immunoglobulins

This may be indicated only if the patient has severe persistent postpartum pemphigoid gestationis or does not respond to oral corticosteroids/corticosteroids, or these are not suitable (e.g. gestational diabetes).

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman is reviewed annually in the Dermatology Clinic. She has multiple skin-coloured and pink- tan soft papules and nodules on her back and several darker brown large macules on her trunk. There are tiny, freckle-like lesions in both axillae. Which of the following is most likely to be found on further investigations or further physical examination?
questions.explanation:
C. Lisch nodules

This patient has neurofibromas, several café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling. This describes neurofibromatosis type 1 (von Recklinghausen's) chromosome 17. Pigmented harmartomas in the iris (Lisch nodules), which do not occur in NF2, are found in 95% of patients.

E. Astrocytoma

Astrocytomas are seen in NF1, but they are rare.

A. Acoustic neuroma

Acoustic neuroma is not classically described in patients with NF1; although case reports exist of it occurring, bilateral acoustic neuromas are seen in NF2 due to a mutation on chromosome 22.

B. Phaeochromocytoma

Phaeochromocytomas occur in about 5% of patients and optic gliomas, astrocytomas and meningiomas may also occur.

D. Charcot's joints

Spinal nerve root involvement may lead to cord compression, muscle wasting and sensory loss (Charcot's joints), although this is relatively rarely seen and is less likely to occur in a young woman of 22.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic. He complains of severe itching over his elbows (see the image below), lower back and his scalp. He has noticed some weeping lesions on his scalp. When questioned, he also admits to feeling more tired recently. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
D. Dermatitis herpetiformis

This can present at any age, typically with severe itching. Lesions begin as vesicles. These are quickly excoriated, so the usual finding is of excoriated papules. These can appear anywhere, though the classical distribution is over extensor surfaces such as the elbows and buttocks. The condition is closely linked with coeliac disease. The diagnosis should be confirmed by histology and immunofluorescence (showing IgA deposition) on skin biopsies. Patients should then be investigated for coeliac disease. Treatment is with a strict gluten-free diet. Resistant cases usually respond to dapsone.

A. Bullous pemphigoid

This is an immunobullous disorder which mostly affects the elderly. It presents with tense bullae and associated erosions.

B. Scabies

This is characteristically intensely pruritic, but does not localise to the sites mentioned in the scenario and almost always spares the scalp.

C. Atopic eczema

This is not incompatible with the history and image shown, but one would expect a history of atopy and it classically affects flexural rather than extensor surfaces.

E. Psoriasis

Although the distribution described would fit very well with psoriasis, this gives rise to well-defined, erythematous plaques with prominent overlying silvery scale.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a very distressing itch. This started nine months ago after the patient moved to a new house. It has been resistant to both hydrocortisone 1% cream and terbinafine cream given to her by her General Practitioner. On examination, there are excoriations, crusts and erosions. The patient insists that her new house is 'infested' and shows 'tracks' on her skin from which she has extracted insects and insect parts, which she brings:: Given the suspected diagnosis, what is the best next management step?
options: A. Two treatments with permethrin cream, one week apart
C. Hibiscrub washes and mupirocin nasal ointment for one week
D. Oral risperidone and psychiatry referral
questions.explanation:
D. Oral risperidone and psychiatry referral

The history and image point to a diagnosis of delusional parasitosis, a psychiatric condition where patients acquire a strong delusional belief that they are infested with parasites. Often the imaginary parasites are described as bugs or insects that are crawling on or under the skin. Any marking on the skin, or particle found on the person or his/her clothing, can be interpreted by the patient as evidence of the parasitic infestation.

Sufferers commonly compulsively gather such samples and present them to medical professionals. This behaviour of evidence gathering is known as the 'matchbox' sign because matchboxes are often used as the container in which samples are being kept by patients. The diagnosis of delusional parasitosis is supported by the fixed views of infestation, even when presented with strong evidence against it. Atypical antipsychotics such as olanzapine or risperidone are currently used as first-line treatment in addition to input from psychiatric services.

Image source: Image source: https://casereports.bmj.com/content/2014/bcr-2013-202850

B. Oral mebendazole

Mebendazole is used to treat parasitic worm infections such as hookworm, making it inappropriate for this patient.

A. Two treatments with permethrin cream, one week apart

Permethrin cream is used in the treatment of scabies. Patients must also take appropriate measures to eradicate the mite from their clothes and bed linen in order to avoid being re-infected.

C. Hibiscrub washes and mupirocin nasal ointment for one week

The combination of hibiscrub washes and mupirocin nasal ointment is a commonly used treatment against colonisation by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

E. Oral fexofenadine

Fexofenadine is a non-sedating antihistamine, commonly used in the treatment of chronic urticaria and allergic rhinitis. 40094

questions.question: A 62-year-old man present to the Dermatology Clinic with the nail lesion shown below, which is diagnosed as a squamous cell carcinoma of the nail. Which of the following viruses is most likely to be the cause?
questions.explanation:
B. HPV 16

Case series suggest that HPV16 is the most common papilloma virus subtype responsible for causing periungual squamous cell carcinoma, the diagnosis here. Other high risk cancer HPV subtypes include 18, 31 and 45.

D. Pox virus

Pox viruses are responsible for development of molluscum contagiosum, not for nail related squamous cell carcinoma.

A. HPV 2

HPV 2 is responsible for common and plantar warts, but is less likely to be a cause of squamous cell carcinoma.

C. HPV 4

HPV 4 is the primary cause of plantar warts.

E. Coxsackie B virus

Coxsackie B is a pathogenic enterovirus and is not linked to the development of nail changes.

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman attends the Dermatology Clinic with a rash on her hands. She has been feeling generally unwell recently, with a series of colds. She works as an animal handler at the local zoo and is concerned that her occupation has led to her condition. The rash is erythematous and occasionally blistering, as shown below: What is the most likely causative organism for her rash?
questions.explanation:
B. Herpes simplex virus (HSV)

The diagnosis here is Erythema multiforme (EM), with target lesions featured in the image. The question is therefore asking simply for the most common underlying cause of EM, which is usually due to an infection.

There is a drug-related cause in around 10% of cases. The most common causative organism for EM is Herpes simplex virus (HSV); therefore, this is the correct answer. Other causes of EM include Mycoplasma pneumoniae, fungal infections and drugs including barbiturates, penicillins, anticonvulsants and non-steroidal anti- inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).

E. Varicella zoster

While varicella zoster is linked to EM, the most common causative organism is HSV. Therefore, varicella zoster is not the correct answer.

A. Cytomegalovirus (CMV)

While Cytomegalovirus (CMV) can cause EM, the most common causative organism is HSV. Therefore, CMV is not the correct answer.

C. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)

While Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) is linked to EM, the most common causative organism is HSV.

Therefore, HIV is not the correct answer.

D. Mycoplasma pneumoniae

Mycoplasma is the second most common cause of EM, after HSV. The most common causative organism is HSV; therefore, Mycoplasma pneumoniae is not the correct answer.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She complains of persistent problems with cracking of the skin at the corners of her mouth. She follows a vegan diet. The cracking at the corners of her mouth is shown below: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her skin changes?
questions.explanation:
A. Riboflavin

Although most vegans are aware of potential vitamin deficiencies and are careful to adequately replace animal sources of B vitamins in their diet, riboflavin (vitamin B 2) deficiency is a possibility and a well-recognised cause of angular stomatitis. Dietary modification with oral supplementation is the most appropriate intervention.

E. Vitamin K

Vitamin K deficiency in adults is rare, as it is ubiquitous in green vegetables. It may occasionally result from malabsorption of fat and can lead to easy bruising and an increased risk of bleeding.

B. Vitamin A

Vitamin A deficiency leads to impaired dark adaptation of vision and dry, scaling skin, which can lead to permanent corneal scarring (keratomalacia) and increased risk of respiratory infection.

C. Vitamin C

Vitamin C deficiency results in the development of scurvy, with follicular keratosis, coiling of hair and perifollicular haemorrhages. There is also an increased risk of lower limb haemorrhage.

D. Vitamin D

Vitamin D deficiency results in the development of osteomalacia, which is manifest in long bone pain and proximal muscle weakness. It is more common in individuals who follow a vegetarian diet.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with a three year history of red, itchy nodules on his left shoulder. He had a previous history of acne vulgaris. He is concerned about the appearance of the lesions. What is the most appropriate next management step?
options: A. Biopsy one of the lesions
E. Reassurance they will resolve over time
questions.explanation:
C. Intra-lesional triamcinolone

The lesions in the photograph are keloid scars, secondary to acne. From the options given, only intra-lesional corticosteroids are likely to drive resolution of the lesions, although there are risks of local bleeding, infection and skin atrophy.

A. Biopsy one of the lesions

A. biopsy is not necessary to confirm the diagnosis, and may worsen any scarring.

B. Oral antihistamine

Although oral antihistamines may reduce itching local irritation, they won't impact on the cosmetic appearance of the lesions.

D. Topical steroid creams

Topical steroid creams only poorly penetrate overlying scarring from the acne.

E. Reassurance they will resolve over time

There is evidence of permanent scarring from the previous acne, which won't resolve over time.

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman presents to the General Medical Clinic as she has noticed itchiness of her scalp. She has previously had eczema as a child but has not suffered from any dermatological problems in adulthood. She has previously had a wide local excision for breast cancer and has maintained remission. She has never smoked. A photograph of her scalp is shown below: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
D. Potent topical corticosteroids

This patient has scalp psoriasis. This is seen as a salmon-pink rash with silvery scales which is usually itchy in nature. Treatment advised by NICE is to first try topical high-potency corticosteroids. Second-line treatment is with topical vitamin D therapy.

B. Salicylic-acid-based shampoo

Salicylic acid is a keratolytic therapy. It can be used to reduce thick scales to allow other treatments to reach the scalp. In the absence of multiple thick scales, it should not be used. It is also not of use as monotherapy.

A. Coal-tar-based shampoo

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has advised that coal-tar-based shampoos should not be used alone for severe cases.

C. Oral corticosteroids

Oral corticosteroids should be avoided in psoriasis. This is because systemic therapy tends to cause rebound psoriasis.

E. Oral griseofulvin

Oral griseofulvin is effective for fungal infections of the scalp such as tinea capitis. These infections show dry scaling with black dots and smooth areas of hair loss. The clinical picture does not match this description.

questions.question: An 18-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a weepy, itchy flexural rash. She has been using potent topical steroids for six months, without much benefit. She thinks she may be allergic to her washing powder. The itching is keeping her awake at night. What is the most appropriate next management step?
options: D. Counselling to help break the scratch itch cycle
questions.explanation:
B. Topical calcineurin inhibitors

Topical calcineurin inhibitors e.g. tacrolimus/pimecrolimus are often used as a steroid alternative, when steroids have stopped working (often due to steroid resistance). They should not be used in pregnancy because of systemic toxicity shown in patients receiving them by the oral route.

E. Topical Calcipotriol

Calcipotriol is a standard therapy for the treatment of psoriasis, not for eczema.

A. Oral Prednisolone

Given the efficacy of steroid sparing topical therapies such as tacrolimus, the benefit risk profile of oral prednisolone versus other options is not considered positive.

C. Skin prick testing

Skin prick testing is not usually helpful in identifying a precipitating allergen in atopic eczema.

D. Counselling to help break the scratch itch cycle

Counselling alone is very unlikely to improve this patients' severe atopic eczema.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with polyuria and malaise. He also complains of a three week history of an erythematous rash in the groin as shown below, which appears to be getting worse. He tells you he has had it intermittently for years but he feels each time he gets it the symptoms are worse. It is very itchy and he is complaining of dysuria. He denies urethral discharge or irritation. He has a regular girlfriend. He is a non-smoker and drinks very little alcohol. Which of the following investigations would be most useful in assessing why he is susceptible to infection?
questions.explanation:
C. Serum fasting glucose

This gentleman's symptoms are suggestive of diabetes, and Candida albicans infections are common in diabetics. A serum fasting glucose of >7 or single random plasma glucose of >11.1 can confirm the diagnosis of diabetes in symptomatic patients. Furthermore, HBA1c can be a diagnostic test; a cut-off point of HBA1c 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) is recommended for diagnosing type 2, but it is not suitable for the diagnosis of suspected type 1 diabetes, which is more likely in this case.

This gentleman has intertrigo. Candida skin infections usually present with soreness and itching and are caused by Candida species.

Risk factors for mucocutaneous candidiasis are: Pregnancy or high-oestrogen contraceptive pill Iron deficiency Underlying skin disease, e.g. psoriasis, dermatitis General debility, e.g. cancer or malnutrition Local factors: heat, moisture, skin maceration, topical corticosteroids, poor dental care Extremes of age Immunocompromised patients, e.g. HIV, chemotherapy, corticosteroid treatment, Cushing's disease Diabetes mellitus.

General management of Candida skin infections includes the following: avoiding occlusion of skin, avoiding obesity, keeping skin dry, washing with emollients as soap substitutes and drying thoroughly after washing.

First-line treatment is usually a topical imidazole cream, e.g. clotrimazole, econazole, ketoconazole or miconazole.

If there is problematic itch or inflammation, consider adding a mild corticosteroid cream for 7-14 days.

Oral fluconazole 50 mg/day for 2-4 weeks if: topical treatment is ineffective or there is widespread infection or if the patient is immunocompromised (depending on the severity of infection and the level of immunocompromise). Review after 2 weeks of fluconazole treatment.

Reference: Eyerich K, Eyerich S, Hiller J, et al; Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, from bench to bedside. Eur J Dermatol. 2010 May/Jun 20(3):260-265. Epub 2010 Feb 5.

A. Syphilis serology

The rash is not suggestive of syphilis, which can present as a painless genital ulcer or a diffuse macular/popular rash involving the whole trunk and extremities.

B. Urine dipstick

Urine dipstick may confirm glycosuria but will not confirm the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus.

D. Urethral swab

If the skin breaks down, this can be associated with dysuria in the absence of a urinary tract infection. There is also no indication that there is any urethral pus.

E. Skin biopsy

Candida albicans (thrush) is usually a clinical diagnosis and does not require skin biopsies. 33381

questions.question: A 32-year-old Nigerian man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with the intensely itchy rash on his neck, shown in the photograph below. He has similar lesions on the trunk and small, hyperpigmented papules on his forearms and wrists. He gives a six month history of these lesions and recently he returned from a trip to Nigeria. He feels well in himself otherwise. He remembers having tuberculosis as a child and was treated for it in Nigeria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
C. Lichen planus

Classical lichen planus is characterised by itchy, violaceous, polygonal, flat-topped papules most commonly developing over the wrists and ankles. A pale, lacy network is often found in the mouth, though this may be asymptomatic. The presence of Wickham's striae - a fine, white lacy pattern over the papules - is characteristic.

The Koebner phenomenon is typically seen in lichen planus (whereby the rash 'colonises' sites of trauma a few days later). Lichen planus has been associated with liver disease including hepatitis C, primary biliary cholangitis and chronic active hepatitis. It usually resolves in 6-18 months. It often responds to potent or very potent topical steroid, but some patients will require oral prednisolone. Lesions tend to resolve to leave deep post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, especially in darker skin-types.

The hypopigmentation seen in this case is attributable to scratching.

E. Keloid scars

Although spontaneous keloids are recognised, the eruption here is too widespread for this and involves sites such as the wrists, where keloids would be most unexpected. Keloids usually have a smooth surface and form nodules or very thickened plaques. Associated itching is not usually severe.

A. Nodular prurigo

This condition is sometimes associated with underlying eczema. Like lichen planus, it is intensely itchy. Nodular lesions are found most commonly on the legs but can occur anywhere on the body. The lesions on the image are plaques rather than nodules; papules on the wrists are often seen in lichen planus.

B. Cutaneous tuberculosis infection

There are various possible manifestations of tuberculosis infection in the skin, but none would be expected to be intensely pruritic.

D. Kaposi's sarcoma

This presents with red, purple or brown cutaneous nodules or plaques, which are usually asymptomatic.

questions.question: A 37-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with hair loss, distributed on the front and crown of her scalp but sparing the sides. She denied using braids, straighteners, tongs or wearing a ponytail. She had no other significant medical problems. How would you best describe this type of alopecia?
questions.explanation:
B. Androgenetic alopecia

Hair loss in this pattern in females may be associated with increased androgens, for example in a patient with polycystic ovarian syndrome, (PCOS). It results in gradual, diffuse thinning over the crown and frontal scalp. A rim of hair is preserved along the frontal margin (in males, this may not be maintained), back and sides of the scalp. (Occipital follicles are not dependent on androgens and are a source for hair transplant.)

C. Telogen effluvium

Telogen effluvium occurs because of sudden entry of hair follicles into the resting phase, resulting in increased hair loss. It is usually associated with acute illness.

A. Cicatricial alopecia

In cicatricial (scarring) alopecia, one would expect to see erythema, scaling, pustules and hyperkeratosis as well as fibrosis.

D. Traction alopecia

Traction alopecia occurs when hair is styled by tightly pulling it back, for example into a pony tail.

E. Alopecia areata

Alopecia areata is autoimmune in origin and results in localised non-scarring alopecia.

questions.question: A 64-year-old woman who has type II diabetes is reviewed on the ward round. She was admitted with cellulitis of the left lower leg some three days earlier. Although her temperature was 38.9 °C on admission, it has now fallen steadily in response to intravenous (IV) co-amoxiclav. The area of cellulitis has reduced in size from a border above her left knee to the mid shin. The erythema has also significantly improved. Her blood culture results are back and there is coagulase-negative staphylococci identified in one bottle, sensitive to vancomycin. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation:
B. Continue Co-amoxiclav

Coagulase-negative staphylococci are one of the most frequently identified bacteria of the normal skin flora. In this situation, with a significant improvement in the clinical picture, the most likely explanation is that the blood culture results are due to contamination. As such, there is no reason to discontinue co-amoxiclav and replace with an anti-staphylococcal agent or to add one to co-amoxiclav. Given her symptoms have significantly improved, she could be switched potentially to oral co-amoxiclav and discharge planning commenced.

E. Switch to Vancomycin

There is no indication to switch to vancomycin here. It has a narrow spectrum of action and is not warranted here, given that overall symptoms of infection are improving.

A. Add Vancomycin

Given this patient is improving, coagulase-negative staphylococci may be a skin contaminant. As such, no change to antibiotic prescribing is needed. iv vancomycin is used for serious staphylococcal infections and in patients with meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA).

C. Switch to Flucloxacillin

Flucloxacillin is rarely an appropriate intervention for bacterial skin infections in diabetes mellitus because of mixed bacterial growth being responsible in the majority of cases. Given the patient's improvement, there is no value in switching therapy.

D. Switch to Linezolid

Linezolid has good tissue penetration and activity against staphylococcal infection. It is of particular value in resistant staphylococcal infection. Here, with improved symptoms overall, it is not required. 39362

questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department (ED) for review. She has cellulitis affecting her left lower leg and says that the area of redness has spread up her leg over the past 24 hours. On examination, she is pyrexial (38 °C), while her blood pressure (BP) is 155/82 mmHg. Her pulse is 85 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. There is erythema over the foot and to the mid-shin on the left leg, with popliteal and inguinal lymphadenopathy. Her body mass index (BMI) is 32 kg/m². Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)129 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)13.1 × 10⁹/l4.0-11.0 × 10⁹/l
Platelets (PLT)207 × 10⁹/l150-400 × 10⁹/l
Sodium (Na+)137 mmol/l135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)4.2 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)102 µmol/l50-120 µmol/l
Fasting glucose4.9 mmol/l< 5.6 mmol/l

Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic therapy?
questions.explanation:
E. Flucloxacillin

Guidelines recommend the use of flucloxacillin in the first instance for uncomplicated cellulitis, in this patient who is non-diabetic.

B. Co-amoxiclav

Co-amoxiclav is the recommended first-line option in cellulitis related to bite injury because of activity against common oral bacteria, and is the default choice in many guidelines for the treatment of cellulitis against a background of diabetes mellitus.

A. Ciprofloxacin

Ciprofloxacin may be added if there is exposure to freshwater at the time of infection because of the risk of infection with organisms such as Pseudomonas. However, quinolone treatment is no longer recommended wherever an effective alternative is available due to a small but significant risk of debilitating adverse effects.

C. Doxycycline

Doxycycline is considered an option for cellulitis where there is significant exposure to salt water.

D. Erythromycin

Macrolides such as erythromycin are the optimal intervention for patients with cellulitis who are allergic to flucloxacillin.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man has a long-standing rash. He thought it had cleared up, but it has recurred in a recent scar from minor surgery. Which of the following conditions exhibits this phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
C. Lichen planus

The appearance of a rash in a scar or in the site of an injury is known as Koebner's phenomenon. The Koebner reaction usually appears around 7-14 days after the injury. Skin disorders that show this reaction include psoriasis, lichen planus and vitiligo. The Koebner response occurs in up to 20% of patients with psoriasis. The term pseudo-Koebner is used for conditions such as molluscum contagiosum and viral warts, where the phenomenon arises from the spread of an infective agent. The reverse Koebner phenomenon also exists where trauma to a lesion results in it resolving.

E. Acne

Acne does not exhibit the Koebner phenomenon, although in individuals prone to acne, application of surgical dressings may lead to development of new lesions underneath where the dressing has been.

A. Eczema

Eczema doesn't exhibit the Koebner phenomenon, and occurs predominantly as an erythematous rash on flexural surfaces.

B. Sarcoid

Sarcoidosis is associated with erythema nodosum, which is seen on the shins and isn't related to local injury.

D. Pemphigoid

Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune skin condition where tense bullae occur, predominantly on areas where skin-to-skin contact may occur such as the upper thighs or the inside of the upper arms.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman, in her third trimester of pregnancy, presents to the Dermatology Clinic with an intensely itchy rash that is keeping her awake at night. The rash started in the stretch marks of her abdomen and is spreading across her buttocks and thighs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Polymorphic Eruption of Pregnancy

Polymorphic Eruption of Pregnancy also known as Pruritic Urticarial Papules and Plaques of Pregnancy (PUPPP) is an itchy eruption that starts in the last 3 months of pregnancy and clears with delivery. It consists of small, pink papules that appear in the stretch marks around the umbilicus. These papules coalesce to form urticarial patches which can spread to involve the buttocks and thighs.

E. Eczema

Eczema is a chronic pruritic condition with characteristic skin changes (inflamed, red, and sometimes weepy patches) that occurs due to a complex interaction between genetic and environmental factors. It usually begins in infancy, but may also occur at any age.

A. Scabies

Scabies is an itchy skin condition that occurs due to infection with the mite Sarcoptes scabiei following prolonged physical contact with an infected person. Scabies is diagnosed clinically due to the presence of burrows, often in typical areas such as the wrists and interdigital spaces of the hands. Treatment is with application of topical permethrin cream.

C. Chronic spontaneous urticaria

Chronic spontaneous urticaria refers to the idiopathic condition where urticarial lesions or angioedema occur in an individual without any inducible cause. Urticaria is usually intensely itchy and may last from a few minutes to 24 hours. The mainstay of treatment is with combinations of oral antihistamines.

D. Lichen planus

Lichen planus is a chronic inflammatory condition of unknown aetiology that typically appears as violaceous plaques with fine, white, lace-like lines (Wickham's striae).

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a 3-month history of an exquisitely painful ulcer on his right shin. This started after an insect bite and rapidly developed into an ulcer. He denies fever but says that the ulcer has been enlarging in size. He has a background of inflammatory bowel disease that is well controlled, with no recent flares. While waiting for his referral, his General Practitioner prescribed a course of topical steroids with limited effect. The other leg is entirely normal. His right leg is examined, as shown below: Which of the following initial treatments is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
E. Topical tacrolimus

This patient has pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) associated with inflammatory bowel disease. The limited disease is typically treated with topical therapies initially to avoid systemic side effects. Following a course of topical steroids, as here, topical calcineurin inhibitors, such as tacrolimus, can result in the resolution of limited PG in up to 50% of patients. It is, therefore, an appropriate second-line option for therapy of limited PG.

Image source: By Raimundo Pastor - Own work, CC BY-SA 4.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?

curid=93865395

A. High-dose oral prednisolone

Systemic corticosteroids are an option for patients with more extensive disease, at daily doses of between 0.5 and 1.5 mg/kg. The risk-benefit profile of systemic corticosteroids means that topical therapies are the usual preferred initial option.

B. Infliximab

Infliximab is an effective biological option for patients who fail to respond to systemic corticosteroids and conventional treatment such as ciclosporin.

C. Oral cyclosporine

Systemic ciclosporin is used as an adjunct to oral corticosteroids in patients who fail to gain an adequate response to therapy.

D. Silver nitrate dressing

Due to the phenomenon of pathergy, use of dressings that may adhere to the area of inflammation, such as silver nitrate, should be avoided.

questions.question: A 27-year-old African-American man presents to the Dermatology Clinic for review. He has a disfiguring scar over his upper abdomen, following a laparotomy six months ago. The scar is causing him to be severely depressed, and he is currently managed with counselling and antidepressants. An image of the scar is shown below: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
questions.explanation:
B. Intralesional triamcinolone

This patient has an extensive keloid scar on his upper abdomen. These are said to occur in up to 16% of patients of African descent. Intralesional steroids flatten and soften the keloid scar and have response rates of > 50%. Where patients fail to respond, other options include 5-FU, and surgery combined with steroid therapy.

A. Cryotherapy

Cryotherapy may be used for keloid scars which do not respond to corticosteroids, either alone or in combination. Direct delivery of liquid nitrogen to the scar itself has improved the effectiveness of cryotherapy, and it is now used earlier in the management of keloid tissue.

C. Intralesional 5-fluorouracil (5-FU)

Intralesional 5-FU is a second-line medical option for patients who fail to respond to intralesional steroids.

D. Surgical excision

Patients who have suffered a keloid scar are much more likely to endure a second episode. Hence surgery is a later treatment option in patients who fail to respond to medical therapy and is combined with steroids in most patients.

E. Targeted radiotherapy

Targeted radiotherapy is effective in reducing keloiding, but in a young man, there is concern about its ability to lead to the development of local skin tumours. It is usually reserved for patients who have undergone surgery for an underlying cancer. 71649

questions.question: A 53-year-old Caucassian man, who previously lived in Australia, is referred to the Dermatology Clinic with a large naevus on his back that has been getting darker in colour. He mentions that his brother was recently diagnosed with a malignant melanoma. Subsequent excision and histology confirms a diagnosis of malignant melanoma with a Breslow thickness of 4 mm. He wishes to know what his prognosis might be. What is the one feature that will most affect his prognosis?
options: B. Location of melanoma on the back
C. Thickness of melanoma at excision
questions.explanation:
C. Thickness of melanoma at excision

The thickness of the melanoma, or Breslow thickness, is the single most important prognostic feature and impacts significantly on management decisions.

Eight-year survival rates for melanoma based on tumour thickness are as follows: < 0.76 mm 93% 0.76-1.69 mm 85% 1.70-3.60 mm 60% > 3.60 mm 33%

E. Change in colour

In order to aid in the diagnosis of melanomas, the ABCDE rule is commonly used. Features that indicate the presence of a melanoma include: Asymmetric shape, Border irregularity, Colour (more than one), Diameter (> 6 mm), and Evolution. The darkening colour of this man's lesion indicates the need for excision, but does not have any impact on prognosis.

A. Family history of melanoma

A. family history of melanoma is a well recognised risk factor for developing melanoma; however, it does not

affect the prognosis once the disease is established.

B. Location of melanoma on the back

In males, the back is the most common area to develop a melanoma, while in women the legs are most commonly affected. The location does not, however, affect prognosis.

D. Previous marked sun exposure

By having lived in Australia, this man has a history of marked sun exposure, which is a well-recognised risk factor for developing melanoma. However, it does not affect the prognosis once the disease is established.8554

questions.question: A 79-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a six week history of a widespread itchy rash. An image of the rash is shown below: It mainly affects the forearms and hands, but there are similar ill-defined, erythematous lesions on the trunk, particularly around the nipples. Her face is unaffected. She lives in a residential home. She feels well in herself otherwise. In addition to her long-term medications, simvastatin and felodipine, she has been taking zopiclone tablets recently prescribed by her GP, to help her sleep. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
D. Scabies

The widespread, itchy eruption, which is worst on the hands, best fits with this diagnosis. Scabies is an infestation with the human scabies mite, Sarcoptes scabiei. It is transmitted by close contact so is often spread between family members, at nurseries and in care institutions. Symptoms occur 4-6 weeks after initial infestation, when hypersensitivity occurs to the mite or its waste products. Scabies is characterised by intense itching, particularly at night. This can lead to prominent excoriation. Burrows (linear crusted lesions of a few millimetres in length) are pathognomonic and penile papules are also highly suggestive, though not always evident. It has a predilection for the web-spaces and around the nipples. Secondary eczematisation is not uncommon, as in this case. Scalp involvement only occurs in young babies and very debilitated adults.

Treatment is usually with permethrin; close contacts should be treated concurrently.

E. Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma

This may present in a variety of ways, including an eczematous eruption. It usually gives rise to well-defined plaques rather than the much more diffuse picture seen here. Sézary syndrome tends to present with erythroderma, in which the skin is deeply erythematous.

A. Folliculitis

This infection, usually due to Staphylococcus aureus, is characterised by pustules.

B. Drug eruption

The rash does not look suggestive of this. Drug eruptions are typically exanthematous (with a maculopapular morphology), and eczematous features are unusual.

C. Atopic eczema

Eczema (in general) may appear at any age, but with no specific pointers to atopy (e.g. history of asthma, childhood eczema, hay fever) and no suggestion of flexural accentuation of the rash, this option is not likely.

questions.question: A 21-year-old professional athlete presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with an itchy rash in his right axilla, shown below: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Tinea axillaris

This is an annular, red lesion with a raised, scaly border, most in keeping with tinea. The rash may well be related to excess sweating linked to sporting activity. Topical azoles are the intervention of choice.

D. Erythrasma

Erythrasma is a superficial skin infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum and occurs in skin folds.

A. Acanthosis nigricans

Acanthosis nigricans is associated with a velvety brown hyperpigmentation of the skin, it is associated with obesity, insulin resistance and gastric carcinoma.

C. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

SLE is associated an erythematous rash which worsens on sun exposure.

E. Epidermal naevus

An epidermal nevus is a benign hamartomatous growth. It presents as a group of verrucous, closely grouped, skin-colored to brown papules and develops in childhood.

questions.question: A 37-year-old man undergoes examination as part of a 'Well Man' screening at his General Practitioner's (GPs) Surgery. The lesion over his heel, shown below, was noted on examination. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation:
A. Fasting lipids

The image shows xanthomata affecting the Achilles tendons. Xanthomata are lesions characterised by accumulations of lipid-laden macrophages, and can be a reflection of lipid metabolism alteration or a result of local cell dysfunction. Tendon xanthomata are diagnostic hallmarks of heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH) (incidence 1 in 500). Other causes of tendon xanthomata are very rare (phytosterolaemia and cerebrotendinous xanthomata), and the presence of raised cholesterol and tendon xanthomata is therefore effectively pathognomonic of FH. The most common sites for tendon xanthomata are in the tendons overlying the Achilles tendons and the knuckles; less common sites include the extensor hallucis longus tendon and the triceps tendon, and they may also occur on the tibial tuberosity at the site of insertion of the patellar tendon (called subperiosteal xanthomata). Ultrasound can be used to look for subclinical Achilles lesions. In heterozygous FH, cholesterol is >7.5 mmol/l and coronary heart disease begins in the third decade; men are at greater risk than women and, if untreated, 50-75% will have a myocardial infarction by the age of 60 years. Homozygous FH presents with coronary disease in the teens and cholesterol levels in excess of 16 mmol/l.

E. Rheumatoid factor

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic systemic inflammatory disease of unknown cause. An external trigger (e.g. cigarette smoking, infection or trauma) that triggers an autoimmune reaction, leading to synovial hypertrophy and chronic joint inflammation along with the potential for extra-articular manifestations, is theorised to occur in genetically susceptible individuals.

The signs on clinical examination include: stiffness tenderness pain on motion swelling deformity limitation of motion extra-articular manifestations rheumatoid nodules.

B. Fasting glucose

Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum is a rash that occurs on the lower legs. It is more common in women, and there are usually several spots. There are also slightly raised shiny, red-brown patches. The centres are often yellowish and may develop open ulcers that are slow to heal.

C. Biopsy of lesion

The diagnosis of the xanthomata is clinical, and ultrasound can be used for confirmation (Achilles lesions).

D. Serum uric acid

Gout and pseudo-gout are the two most common crystal-induced arthropathies. Gout is caused by monosodium urate monohydrate crystals; pseudo-gout is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals and is more accurately termed calcium pyrophosphate disease. Physical findings may include the following: involvement of a single (most common) or multiple joints signs of inflammation - swelling, warmth, erythema (sometimes resembling cellulitis) and tenderness fever (also consider infectious arthritis) migratory polyarthritis (rare) posterior interosseous nerve syndrome (rare) tophi in soft tissues (helix of the ear, fingers, toes, prepatellar bursa, olecranon) eye involvement - tophi, crystal-containing conjunctival nodules, band keratopathy, blurred vision, anterior uveitis (rare), scleritis.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman is being investigated for an erythematous, scaly malar rash. She feels generally unwell, with frequent mouth ulcers and intermittent arthralgia of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints for the past few months. She also reports lack of appetite and has lost 5 kg in weight over the last six weeks. Which of the following tests is the most specific to the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
C. dsDNA antibodies

This patient already describes three criteria for SLE (> 4/11 are required to make a diagnosis, although these do not have to be present simultaneously). A high titre of dsDNA antibodies is virtually exclusive to SLE and would confirm this diagnosis. Titres can be used to measure disease activity.

E. Serum complement

Complement levels, ESR and dsDNA titres can be used to monitor disease activity in SLE.

A. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)

Raised ESR values are not diagnostic of SLE, but seen across multiple inflammatory conditions. ESR values can be used to monitor disease activity in SLE.

B. C-reactive protein (CRP)

CRP is not particularly useful in SLE, as levels may remain low in active disease.

D. Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs)

ANAs are autoantibodies that bind to contents of the cell nucleus. They are encountered in many conditions such as SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, dermatomyositis, autoimmune hepatitis and primary biliary cholangitis.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with complaints of facial flushing and a gradual change of complexion for the past two years. She reports exacerbation of these symptoms on the consumption of spicy food and alcohol. She also mentions burning and stinging when working out in the gym. What would be the first line of management for this patient?
options: A. Limit exposure to known aggravating factors
questions.explanation:
A. Limit exposure to known aggravating factors

This patient is suffering from acne rosacea. The best advice for people with rosacea is to limit exposure to known aggravating factors such as alcohol, sun exposure, hot drinks and spicy food, especially in this patient with erythemato-telangiectatic rosacea.

E. Topical ivermectin

Topical ivermectin should only be considered in patients with papulopustular rosacea.

B. Oral tetracycline

Oral antibiotics should only be considered as a first-line treatment option for more severe papulopustular rosacea.

C. Topical brimonidine

Topical brimonidine is considered in people with rosacea where the main presenting feature is facial erythema.

D. Topical isotretinoin

It would be appropriate to limit exposure to known aggravating factors, rather than using pharmacological interventions, in this patient with erythemato-telangiectatic rosacea.

questions.question: A 67-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a mole on her back, which she believes has changed. She feels that it has got somewhat darker, particularly after a recent holiday in the Caribbean. She is fair-skinned and has attended the clinic previously for numerous other moles, none of which have been treated. The mole, as shown below, is 19 mm × 43 mm. It measures 2.13 mm in thickness. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
options: E. Local excision with 2 cm margin
questions.explanation:
E. Local excision with 2 cm margin

This lesion is irregular in diameter, colour and symmetry. This raises high suspicion of malignant melanoma. The most important management step to remember here is that melanoma is managed with local excision. The extent of margin clearance is dependent on the staging based on the American Joint Committee on Cancer's (AJCC) Melanoma of skin staging. In this case, with a stage 2 melanoma a 2 cm clearance is required as per NICE guidelines.

D. Undertake a 3-mm punch biopsy

While a punch biopsy would be a useful step in a suspected malignant lesion, this lesion is particularly worrying for melanoma, given its irregular features. Therefore, it would be appropriate to move straight to a wider excision of this lesion, so that margins can be well assessed.

A. Moh's micrographic surgery

Moh's micrographic surgery is a surgical technique through which tissue is removed and examined for both cells present and the margins. This occurs while the patient waits and informs the decision for further tissue removal.

This tends to be used for basal cell carcinoma or other less worrying tumours and is not first line for melanoma, the lesion in this question.

B. Reassure and discharge

This lesion is irregular in diameter, colour and symmetry. This raises high suspicion of malignant melanoma.

Melanoma is managed with wide local excision. It would be very dangerous to discharge this patient without treatment.

C. Treat with topical 5-fluorouracil

The most likely cause of this lesion is malignant melanoma. Topical 5-fluorouracil may be an effective treatment for actinic keratoses, which are squamous cell carcinomas in situ. Topical 5-fluorouracil would not be an appropriate management step for melanoma.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman presents with a dark, irregularly shaped lesion on her upper back that has grown in size over the last six months. She reports occasional itching and a recent episode of bleeding from the lesion after accidental trauma. On examination, the lesion is asymmetrical, with uneven borders and multiple colours ranging from brown to black, and has a diameter of approximately 9 mm. There are no palpable lymph nodes. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: B. Wide local excision of the lesion
C. Excisional biopsy with a 2-mm margin
D. Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion
E. Punch biopsy of the lesion
questions.explanation:
C. Excisional biopsy with a 2-mm margin

The most likely diagnosis is malignant melanoma. An excisional biopsy with narrow margins allows for complete histopathological evaluation of the lesion to confirm the diagnosis and assess the depth, an essential parameter for staging melanoma.

E. Punch biopsy of the lesion

A. punch biopsy may miss important features of melanoma such as the lesion's full depth or heterogeneity. It is

less ideal than an excisional biopsy for diagnosing melanoma.

A. Dermoscopy of the lesion

Dermoscopy is a non-invasive diagnostic tool that provides a magnified view of the lesion and can help to identify features suggestive of melanoma (eg atypical pigment network, asymmetry). However, it does not provide a definitive diagnosis, which requires histopathological examination.

B. Wide local excision of the lesion

Wide local excision is part of the treatment plan for confirmed melanoma where margins of 1-2 cm are taken, depending on the thickness of the tumour. It is not used for initial diagnosis.

D. Fine-needle aspiration of the lesion

Fine-needle aspiration is typically used for sampling lymph nodes or masses suspected of metastasis, not for primary diagnosis of skin lesions.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a 7-month history of rough and dry skin, particularly over her lower limbs. She noticed that her symptoms were worse in winter but always present. She has tried moisturising with supermarket body creams but has found that it makes little difference and affects her confidence. Her past medical history includes type I diabetes mellitus, for which she takes regular insulin therapy. However, her blood sugars have been poorly controlled over the past year. Her legs are examined and shown below: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
C. Ichthyosis vulgaris

Taking a look at this patient's legs, there is evidence of hyperkeratosis and scaling of the skin. However, there is no visual erythema, excoriations or inflammatory changes. This is likely representative of ichthyosis vulgaris.

Ichthyosis refers to dry and scaly skin and can be inherited or acquired. Inherited causes tend to present at an early age, while acquired causes are associated with conditions such as diabetes mellitus, lymphoma and systemic lupus erythematosus. Therefore, the history of diabetes mellitus makes ichthyosis more likely.

Stronger paraffin-containing emollients tend to be useful in managing the condition, as well as treating the underlying cause (if acquired).

D. Keratosis pilaris

Keratosis pilaris is a common dermatological condition characterised by a 'goose flesh'-like appearance to skin secondary to multiple follicular keratotic papules with or without associated erythema. It affects anywhere hair grows, so it can occur on all skin surfaces, but is most prevalent on the extremities

A. Asteatotic dermatitis

Asteatotic dermatitis (eczema craquelé) is a cause of dry, cracked skin. The condition most commonly affects the elderly population with the usual presentation being of an elderly patient complaining of dry and itchy skin in the colder months. The legs, arms and trunk are most commonly affected. The appearance of the skin is cracked with excoriation and erythema. Therefore, asteatotic dermatitis will have appearances of superimposed inflammation in contrast to other cracked skin conditions, such as ichthyosis vulgaris as seen in this patient.

B. Atopic eczema

Atopic eczema is an inflammatory skin disorder characterised by dry, exfoliative skin changes associated with erythema, scaling and pruritis. It is a common condition and, therefore, a reasonable differential diagnosis.

However, the lack of exfoliative or erythematous skin changes makes an alternative diagnosis more likely.

E. Lichen planus

Lichen planus is an idiopathic inflammatory dermatological condition that causes an eruption of itchy and shiny papules over the extremities that often have a violaceous colour. These lesions are often itchy and can also affect the mucous membranes and genitalia. These lesions are not seen here, making this diagnosis unlikely.

questions.question: A 31-year-old woman, who is a nursery worker with a history of periorbital eczema, presents to her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of a rash on her right cheek. The rash has been present for about a week but began as a small blister which subsequently ruptured. The patient had thought that it had been an insect bite but became more concerned as the area affected began to increase in size with a similar perioral lesion in the last few days, seen below. Although the lesion is painless, the patient does complain of burning and itching over the rash. The patient is otherwise fit and well and is not on any medications. She lives alone and does not recall being in contact with anyone with a similar rash. On examination, the patient has a weeping area measuring 4 cm across her right cheek with golden, crusted edges. General examination of the patient was otherwise normal and no other lesions were identified. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Impetigo

Atopic skin is prone to acquiring superimposed bacterial and viral infections. Impetigo is an acute and highly contagious superficial infection of the skin that commonly occurs in children, and consequently outbreaks in nurseries and schools are not rare. The pustules and yellow coloured crusted erosions in the peri-oral area here are classical. There are two forms of the condition, bullous and non-bullous, with the former being caused almost exclusively by Staphylococcus aureus whereas the latter can be caused by S. aureus, group A streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes), or a combination of both. Culture of the skin lesions is required to confirm the diagnosis and determine the causative organism. Treatment can consist of topical therapy (topical mupirocin) alone or in combination with systemic therapy.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:OSC_Microbio_21_02_impetigo.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:OSC_Microbio_21_02_impetigo.jpg)

C. Herpes simplex infection

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection can cause a variety of clinical symptoms. HSV type 1 is normally associated with orofacial infections. It typically presents as vesicular rash that may be preceded by a prodrome of pain, tingling, burning or itching. Vesicles become pustular or ulcerative with formation of crusts within 72- 96 hours and heal over 8-10 days.

A. Erysipelas

Erysipelas is a superficial bacterial skin infection caused by S. pyogenes and characterized by well demarcated erythema. Lymphatic involvement is common and manifests by streaking of the overlying skin and local lymphadenopathy.

D. Herpes zoster infection

Primary herpes zoster infection causes chickenpox. The virus becomes latent and upon reactivation causes shingles (a painful, vesicular rash in a dermatomal distribution).

E. Atopic dermatitis

AD is a chronic pruritic condition with characteristic skin changes (inflamed, red, and sometimes weepy patches) that occurs due to a complex interaction between genetic and environmental factors. It usually begins in infancy, but may also occur at any age. Atopic skin is prone to acquiring superimposed infections, commonly with either HSV (eczema herpeticum) or S. Aureus (impetigo). 7612

questions.question:
A 27-year-old man of Chinese origin is commenced on Carbamazepine for complex partial seizures. He presents to the Emergency Department (ED) a few days later complaining of upper respiratory tract infection (RTI) symptoms, and severe ulceration affecting his mouth and lips. On examination, his temperature is 38.2°C. His blood pressure (BP) is 115/82 mmHg, while his pulse is 80 beats per minute (bpm) and regular. You confirm a number of ulcers within the oropharynx. He has a number of target lesions over the surface of his body, some of which have ulcerated with a necrotic centre. In certain areas the lesions have become confluent, with wider areas of skin loss. Investigations reveal the following:

InvestigationResultNormal values
Haemoglobin (Hb)131 g/l135-175 g/l
White cell count (WCC)11.2 × 10⁹/l4.0-11.0× 10⁹/l
Platelets (PLT)201×10⁹/l150-400× 10⁹/l
Sodium (Na+)137 mmol/l135-145 mmol/l
Potassium (K+)4.0 mmol/l3.5-5.0 mmol/l
Creatinine (Cr)110 µmol/l50-120µmol/l
Glucose5.1 mmol/l3.9-7.1 mmol/l
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)65mm/hour 1-20 mm/hour

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
E. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome

The answer is Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) - SJS is recognised to occur in patients prescribed Carbamazepine, particularly in patients of Chinese origin who are HLA B1502 positive. The severe mucosal ulceration, coupled with target lesions and wider areas of erythema is consistent with the diagnosis. Often patients complain of upper respiratory tract symptoms at the same time as skin / mucosal lesions appear. Removal of the offending agent is the key intervention with supportive therapy to maintain fluid balance and prevent infection where possible. Use of corticosteroids in managing the condition is the subject of debate.

B. Bullous pemphigoid

Bullous pemphigoid is incorrect, it is associated with a blistering skin rash which is more commonly associated with flexural skin and mucosal surfaces. It is not usually associated with the prodrome of upper respiratory tract infection seen here, or with Carbamazepine therapy.

A. Behçet's disease

Behçet's disease, is incorrect, it is associated with mucosal ulceration, uveitis and arthritis. It tends to relapse and remit, it is unlikely to occur in such close proximity to the Carbamazepine start.

C. Legionella pneumonia infection

Legionella pneumonia infection, is incorrect, it is associated with pleuritic chest pain without dermatological manifestations as seen here.

D. Pemphigus vulgaris

Pemphigus vulgaris, is incorrect, it is much more protracted in onset, with oral lesions usually appearing first, skin lesions being seen up to 4 months later.

questions.question: A 78-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with an erythematous rash which has gradually increased in severity over the past seven months. The rash forms concentric erythematous bands, very much like the wood grains you would see on a tree. He has a chronic cough, thought to be related to previous cigarette smoking, although he gave up some 30 years earlier, and has had an operation for an inguinal hernia some five years earlier. Which of the following is the most likely underlying malignancy?
options: E. Squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus
questions.explanation:
E. Squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus

This rare skin condition is erythema gyratum repens, which is most often seen in association with squamous cell carcinoma of the bronchus. It may also be seen in association with oesophageal and breast cancer, although the difficulty with a cough is a stronger pointer towards lung cancer.

A. Gastric carcinoma

Gastric cancer is associated with acanthosis nigricans.

B. Oesophageal carcinoma

Although oesophageal carcinoma is associated with erythema gyratum repens, it is less likely here given the absence of symptoms of indigestion.

C. Pancreatic carcinoma

Pancreatic carcinoma is associated with thrombophlebitis migrans.

D. Small cell lung cancer

Skin rashes are not a usual phenomenon associated with small cell lung cancer. 38310

questions.question: A 32-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic for review. He has an annular, scaling lesion some 4 cm in diameter affecting his right forefoot. He has a history of type I diabetes, well-controlled on a basal bolus insulin regime. His most recent HbA1c has been measured at 51 mmol/mol (6.8%). Apparently, the General Practitioner (GP) has prescribed oral co-amoxiclav and topical fusidic acid ointment, although these have been ineffective. The lesion is shown below. Which of the following interventions is most appropriate?
questions.explanation:
E. Ketoconazole cream

The image reveals a pink, annular, scaling skin lesion of the patient's thigh which fits best with tinea infection.

Most cases respond to topical Imidazole therapy over a course of 3-4 weeks. In those that do not respond, oral Itraconazole would be the next step or terbinafine as a second-line option.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tinea_corporis.png (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tinea_corporis.png) - Public domain

D. Oral terbinafine

Terbinafine is an effective second-line option for tinea infections, first-line treatment is oral imidazoles such as itraconazole.

A. Oral flucloxacillin

The description of the lesions is typical of fungal infections and therefore flucloxacillin would not be appropriate.

B. Oral itraconazole

Most cases of tinea infections respond to topical treatment and therefore systemic treatment is not appropriate as a first-line treatment option.

C. Oral griseofulvin

Griseofulvin is usually reserved for the treatment of fungal infections in children and therefore is not an appropriate treatment option.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with an asymptomatic rash on his face, which has been present for several years. He is well in himself, although has a history of iron deficiency anaemia. He says that he feels fit and well. He takes amlodipine, pravastatin and ferrous sulphate regularly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia

This is an autosomal, dominantly inherited condition. Small dilated blood vessels manifest as red macules and papules, visible around the mouth, and on the lips and fingers. Lesions also occur on mucous membranes and in the gastrointestinal tract: these may be associated with severe epistaxis and gastrointestinal bleeding. Anaemia due to bleeding is treated with oral iron. The cutaneous involvement does not need any treatment, although vascular lasers are usually effective for symptomatic lesions.

C. Limited systemic sclerosis

This used to be termed CREST syndrome (calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, oesophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly or telangiectasia). Facial telangiectasia, including of the oral mucosa, is a feature, but the absence of other symptoms or signs in this case makes HHT a better response.

B. Peutz-Jegher syndrome

This is another rare, genetically determined condition that is characterised by pigmented macules on the lips, the skin around the mouth and the fingers and toes, occurring early in childhood. It is associated with small bowel polyps, which can cause intussusception. The gene confers a high risk of developing internal cancers, not only developing from intestinal polyps, but also in many other organs.

D. Idiopathic thrombocytopenia purpura

Any cause of thrombocytopenia may result in purpura, but the discrete, fixed lesions confined to the face seen here are more in keeping with telangiectasia.

E. Rosacea

This is an acneiform disorder which usually presents with facial papules and pustules. These may be on a background of diffuse telangiectasia. The discrete lesions shown in the image, with an absence of inflammatory changes, are more suggestive of HHT.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with symmetrical, elevated dark pink lesions over both shins. The lesions have a shiny, orange peel appearance. She has lost 4 kg in weight over the past six months and she has recently developed atrial fibrillation (AF). Which of the following is most likely to be found on hand examination?
questions.explanation:
C. Acropachy

These lesions describe pretibial myxoedema, which occurs in 5% of patients with Graves' disease. It is almost always accompanied by exophthalmos and occasionally thyroid acropachy.

E. Leukonychia

Leukonychia is seen in patients suffering from hypoalbuminaemia - for example, in chronic liver disease.

A. Nail pitting

Nail pitting and onycholysis are most likely to be associated with psoriasis, although onycholysis may also be seen in patients with thyroid disease.

B. Koilonychia

Koilonychia is derived from the Greek, denoting spoon-shaped nails, seen as a result of iron deficiency anaemia.

D. Deforming hand arthritis

Deforming hand arthritis is seen in rheumatoid disease and in psoriasis, neither of which are associated with pre-tibial myxoedema. 9197

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman with psoriasis attends your Dermatology Clinic. She has tried multiple creams and has had several courses of ultraviolet B (UVB) therapy. During the consultation, she is tearful and frustrated, stating the psoriasis is 'taking over her life' and ruining her social life and self-esteem. She is reluctant to consider systemic therapies that would weaken her immune system. You feel that acitretin may be a good option for her and ask her about her desire to have children. She states that, although she is currently in a relationship, she has no plans to start a family. How long would she have to avoid pregnancy after taking acitretin?
questions.explanation:
E. 3 Years

Manufacturer's guidelines state that the time required to avoid pregnancy with acitretin is 3 years. The prescribing information states that pregnancy must be reliably prevented 4 weeks before, during and for 3 years after the completion of therapy. Advice on contraception is also given to males starting therapy who are sexually active. Isotretinoin and alitretinoin must be discontinued at least 1 month before pregnancy.

A. 1 Week

For any medication with potential effects on pregnancy, contraceptive precautions must be continued for at least one cycle. As such, 1 week is considered too short.

B. 2 Weeks

Two weeks is less than the duration of a single menstrual cycle and is therefore inappropriate advice with respect to avoidance of conception for any medication which may impact on successful pregnancy.

C. 1 Month

One month is the length of a single menstrual cycle; like 1 week and 2 weeks, 1 month is therefore considered too short a period of avoidance of conception.

D. 6 Months

Six months is the recommended period of pregnancy avoidance after methotrexate therapy.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with the skin lesion shown below on the anterior aspect of her shin. She thinks that is increasing in size. She also attends another hospital for diabetes mellitus, for which she takes a combination of metformin and sitagliptin. Over the past few months, she admits to increasing tiredness and vague joint pains. On examination, her blood pressure (HP) is 149/82 mmHg. Her pulse is 72 beats per minute (bpm) and regular and her body mass index (BMI) is 29 kg/m². Which is the most likely cause of her skin lesion?
questions.explanation:
E. Necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum

Early necrobiosis lipoidica diabeticorum is often difficult to diagnose as it may appear psoriatic in nature, and telangiectasia are seen on the waxy surface. Less than 1% of diabetic patients have this, but most patients with the condition have diabetes mellitus (60%). Lesions appear as one or more discoloured areas on the fronts of the shins - shiny, atrophic and brown-red or slightly yellow. The margin may be erythematous or violet.

Treatment is difficult, although anti-platelet agents and immunomodulators appear to show at least some effect on progression.

B. Sarcoidosis

Sarcoidosis is associated with erythema nodosum, with multiple raised red/purple nodules on the shins, rather than the single enlarging lesion seen here.

A. Psoriasis

A. single lesion on the shin is unlikely to be due to psoriasis, and the size increase is consistent with necrobiosis

lipoidica.

C. Basal cell carcinoma

Sun-exposed areas of skin, such as the head and neck, are the commonest areas for basal cell carcinomas to occur. They may resemble necrobiosis in the early stages, although a more nodular appearance versus that seen here would be expected.

D. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

SLE is associated with erythema nodosum and arthritis, but other features such as a rash on sun-exposed areas of skin are not seen here.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with the rash shown below. His mother also suffers from a similar skin condition. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
C. Neurofibromatosis

The picture shows multiple cutaneous neurofibromata.

Criteria for the diagnosis of neurofibromatosis are: six or more café-au-lait spots two or more neurofibromas axillary freckling two or more Lisch nodules (iris hamartomata) optic glioma a parent or sibling with neurofibromatosis.

Associated abnormalities include: skeletal rib notching and other bony defects honeycomb lung intellectual disability kyphoscoliosis hypertension (renal artery stenosis, phaeochromocytoma).

D. Dercum's disease

Dercum's disease also known as adiposis dolorosa is of unknown aetiology and characterised by a combination of lipomas, painful subcutaneous plaques and non-traumatic ecchymoses.

A. Eruptive xanthomas

Eruptive xanthomas are rapidly occurring crops of small, red-yellow papules that commonly occur over the buttocks, shoulders, arms and legs. Lesions may be tender and itchy and are associated with hypertriglyceridaemia.

B. Tuberous sclerosis
