Features of tuberous sclerosis include angiofibromata, ash-leaf macules, shagreen patches and periungual fibromata. The condition may also be associated with epilepsy and cognitive impairment.

E. Keratosis pilaris

Keratosis pilaris is a very common form of dry skin, characterised by hair follicle plugging due to excess keratin.

It most often affects the outer aspect of the forearms but may also occur in other sites in a symmetrical distribution.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She has gained 15 kg in weight over the past year and is very concerned about her appearance due to numerous striae across her abdomen and upper thighs. She has a past history of asthma, for which she takes salbutamol as required. She admits to overeating and drinks 1-2 bottles of wine per week. On examination, her BP is 155/92 mmHg and her heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. She has marked truncal obesity, with a BMI of 33 kg/m². She also finds it difficult to get up out of a chair in the clinic without using her arms. Investigations

InvestigationResultNormal Values
Haemoglobin (Hb)131 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)7.1 ×10⁹/L4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L
Platelets (PLT)189 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Sodium (Na⁺)143 mmol/L135–145 mmol/L
Potassium (K⁺)3.4 mmol/L3.5–5.0 mmol/L
Creatinine (Cr)95 µmol/L50–120 µmol/L
Fasting glucose7.3 mmol/L<5.6 mmol/L
Random cortisol621 nmol/L280–700 nmol/L
0900 h cortisol post-overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test150 nmol/L<50 nmol/L
Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)2 U/L1–7 U/L
Luteinising hormone (LH)1 U/L1.25–7.80 U/L
Plasma corticotropin (ACTH)7 pmol/L2.2–13.3 pmol/L
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Cushing's disease

Clinical features with Cushing syndrome, such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, marked truncal obesity and proximal myopathy, are all present here. The key differentiator is that the adrenocorticotropin hormone (ACTH) is not suppressed and cortisol is not suppressed by dexamethasone, which immediately alerts us to a potential ACTH-producing pituitary adenoma. The reduction in luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels are other potential clues to pituitary-dependent Cushing's disease.

A. Adrenal adenoma

Adrenal adenoma is unlikely here because although the dexamethasone suppression test suggests Cushing syndrome, the fact that ACTH is not suppressed effectively means this must be due to a pituitary adenoma.

C. Non-functioning pituitary adenoma

Non-functioning adenoma is incorrect because although the LH and FSH levels are low, the ACTH level is elevated and is driving elevated cortisol levels, which is highly suggestive of an ACTH-producing tumour.

D. Pseudo-Cushing's disease

Pseudo-Cushing's disease presents similarly to Cushing's disease. However, rather than an endogenous cause of raised cortisol levels and corticosteroids, pseudo-Cushing's disease is associated with chronic alcohol excess.

This patient drinks 1-2 bottles of wine a week, equivalent to 10-20 units, which is unlikely to be enough to cause this clinical picture.

E. Type II diabetes

Type II diabetes mellitus is unlikely here. Although this patient is overweight and has a raised glucose level, the diagnosis does not explain this patient's abnormal dexamethasone suppression test or other clinical features such as proximal myopathy.

questions.question: A 19-year-old man is referred to the Neurology Outpatient Department by his General Practitioner (GP), who suspects that he may have neurofibromatosis (NF). He is of short stature and has mild learning difficulties. He also suffers from mild hypertension. A photograph of the affected area is shown below. Which of the following combinations of criteria would establish the diagnosis in this patient?
options: A. Six or more café-au-lait macules > 5 mm and axillary freckling
B. Six or more café-au-lait macules > 15 mm and the presence of a juvenile cataract
C. Two or more neurofibromas of any type and a Lisch nodule
D. Sphenoid dysplasia and two or more Lisch nodules
E. Renal artery stenosis and freckling in the inguinal region
questions.explanation:
D. Sphenoid dysplasia and two or more Lisch nodules

Sphenoid wing dysplasia is characteristic, but not pathognomonic of type 1 NF. In company with Lisch nodules, this is consistent with a diagnosis of type 1 NF.

A. Six or more café-au-lait macules > 5 mm and axillary freckling

Type 1 NF (von Recklinghausen's disease) is an autosomal dominant condition with variable expression. The affected gene is on chromosome 17. Mild learning difficulties are common in these patients, and hypertension may occur in association with renal artery stenosis or phaeochromocytoma.

The diagnosis of NF in this adult patient fails to meet the following criterion: six or more café-au-lait macules > 15 mm in size.

B. Six or more café-au-lait macules > 15 mm and the presence of a juvenile cataract

The presence of juvenile cataracts does not form part of the diagnostic criteria for type 1 NF.

C. Two or more neurofibromas of any type and a Lisch nodule

Two or more Lisch nodules would need to be present for the diagnosis of type 1 NF to be made.

E. Renal artery stenosis and freckling in the inguinal region

The diagnosis of type 1 NF is made of two or more of the following criteria present: six or more café-au-lait macules > 5 mm (prepubertal) or > 15 mm (post-pubertal) two or more neurofibromas of any type or one plexiform freckling in the axillary or inguinal regions optic glioma two or more Lisch nodules on the iris distinctive osseous lesion typical of type 1 NF, eg sphenoid dysplasia, thickening of the long bone cortex with or without pseudo-arthrosis a first-degree relative with type 1 NF.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man is reviewed in the Emergency Department (ED) having presented with lethargy. While examining him, you notice the rash in the image shown below. He tells you that occasionally it is itchy, but it has been there for at least four years. He has a family history of vitiligo. He is a non-smoker and drinks no alcohol. He takes no medications regularly and has no allergies. Physical examination, apart from the rash, is normal. He is keen to improve the appearance. What is the most appropriate management option?
options: A. Wash with ketoconazole body wash
B. Referral to a dermatologist for skin biopsy
D. Reassure the patient and advise no treatment is available
questions.explanation:
A. Wash with ketoconazole body wash

This diagnosis here is pityriasis versicolor. This is caused by overgrowth of the (usually) commensal yeast, Malassezia furfur. It typically presents in young adults in warm weather or after a sunny holiday, with asymptomatic hypo- or sometimes hyperpigmented macules with very fine peripheral scaling. It is usually confined to the trunk. The diagnosis should be confirmed mycologically on a skin scraping. It may respond to topical antifungal treatment, such as washing with ketoconazole body wash. Other options include antifungal creams, or itraconazole 200 mg once daily for a week. Patients should be advised that the pigmentation may take months to return to normal after successful treatment.

Pityriasis versicolor is sometimes confused with vitiligo. The latter causes depigmentation rather than hypopigmentation, usually affecting much larger areas than the 1 cm lesions of pityriasis versicolor. The hands, face and genitalia are fairly commonly affected in vitiligo, but not in pityriasis versicolor. Scaling does not occur in vitiligo.

B. Referral to a dermatologist for skin biopsy

This condition is usually a simple clinical diagnosis which can be confirmed via a skin scraping.

C. Moderate-potency topical corticosteroid

Topical steroids are ineffective for this condition and might make it worse.

D. Reassure the patient and advise no treatment is available

Whilst reassurance is appropriate, pityriasis versicolor can usually be treated fairly simply, though it may recur.

E. Oral prednisolone

This has no role in the treatment of a yeast infection.

questions.question: A 42-year-old Egyptian man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with changes on his nose which have developed over a period of 10 years. Further examination reveals no further skin lesions or regional lymphadenopathy. He was seen when in Cairo by his usual doctor, who told him that there was little he could do about the end of his nose, which has considerably worsened in appearance over the past few months. It does not give him any trouble, but he finds it unsightly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
C. Lupus vulgaris

This is a chronic tuberculous infection of the skin, which is now very rare in developed countries. It presents as a slowly enlarging, infiltrated plaque. Diagnosis may be possible on histology or via tissue culture. Treatment is the same as that for pulmonary tuberculosis.

A. Tularaemia

This tick-borne bacterial infection is endemic in Egypt. There are various types of presentation, including chronic skin ulceration. Over time, this tends to heal with scarring. Lymphadenopathy tends to be prominent in this condition.

B. Lupus pernio

This is a subtype of sarcoidosis. The nose and ears are common sites, but it is usually associated with deep- seated inflammation. The colour is violaceous or mauve and there is little surface change.

D. Basal cell carcinoma

This is commoner in lighter skin types. It does usually progress very slowly if untreated. The lesion in the image lacks specific features of this diagnosis (pearly, rolled edge; telangiectasia).

E. Squamous cell carcinoma

The history is too long for this, as SCC would likely have become more nodular or ulcerated by this time, as well as probably metastasising to local lymph nodes. The tissue distortion would not be compatible with SCC-in situ (Bowen's disease).

questions.question: An 18-year-old, fit and healthy woman of normal body weight is about to be treated with isotretinoin for scarring acne. Which of the following is most important before starting therapy?
questions.explanation:
D. Negative pregnancy testing

Isotretinoin is highly teratogenic. Effective contraception must therefore be instituted at least one month before starting therapy, and a negative pregnancy test witnessed before treatment is commenced. Patients who become pregnant while on therapy should be offered a termination.

E. Weight control

Isotretinoin may precipitate benign intracranial hypertension in some patients who use it. We are told this patient is fit and well with a normal body weight, and measures to control weight gain are therefore unlikely to be needed.

A. Low-cholesterol diet

Although treatment with isotretinoin may precipitate elevations in LDL and triglycerides, no dietary intervention is required. Baseline testing of lipid profile is recommended.

B. Monitoring of renal function

Renal function does not affect metabolism of isotretinoin and no dose adjustment is recommended. Liver function testing, in contrast, is recommended for patients commencing isotretinoin therapy.

C. Use of sun screen

Intense sun exposure can lead to hypersensitivity rashes in patients taking isotretinoin, and sun screen is advised, although this clearly is not as crucial an intervention as pregnancy testing.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman who has Raynaud's phenomenon and gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She is very concerned about the cosmetic appearance of her neck, which is shown in the image below: Current medications of note include amlodipine and lisinopril, which she takes for control of high blood pressure (BP). On examination, there is thickening of the skin over her hands and several telangiectasia over the upper chest. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
E. Systemic sclerosis

The picture shows significant skin thickening over the anterior neck, which is consistent with systemic sclerosis.

The Raynaud's phenomenon, skin changes over the hands, telangiectasia, reflux and hypertension also support the diagnosis.

C. Morphoea

Morphoea is localised scleroderma, which would not fit with the generalised symptoms this patient has, including Raynaud's phenomenon, hypertension and GORD.

A. Acquired ichthyosis (AI)

AI is associated with dry skin and severe skin scaling, rather than thickening as seen here. It is associated with the development of lymphoma in older adults.

B. Lupus vulgaris

Lupus vulgaris is the skin manifestation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, which appears as painful nodular skin lesions. They are seen around the neck and may also be seen on the face.

D. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

SLE is associated with small joint polyarthritis and photosensitive rash, as opposed to the picture seen here with predominant skin thickening.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman attends her General Practitioner (GP) after developing a flaccid blistering over her face, axillae and groins, which rupture to leave painful erosions. She also complains of a painful mouth. Biopsy with immunofluorescence shows immunoglobulin deposition throughout the epidermis. Given the likely diagnosis, what is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation:
A. Prednisolone 0.5-1.5 mg/kg od

This woman has classic features of pemphigus vulgaris. The blisters are flaccid and commonly affect mucosal membranes. In contrast, bullous pemphigoid presents with tense blisters and immunofluorescence along the basement membrane. Patients require high-dose oral steroids to induce remission; however, the optimal steroid dosing has not been fully validated yet. Patients often also require long-term lower dose steroids for maintenance, usually for around two years. The severity and history of the condition are variable. Prior to the use of steroids the condition used to have a high mortality, which has now been reduced to 5-15%.

E. Amoxicillin 500 mg tds

Amoxicillin is an antibiotic and not indicated in the treatment of pemphigus vulgaris. In the case of acquiring a superimposed skin infection, alternative antibiotics such as flucloxacillin are commonly used.

B. Prednisolone 10 mg od

Higher doses of oral steroids are required in order to induce remission; however, lower doses may be used in long-term in order to maintain remission.

C. Topical steroids

Oral, and not topical, steroids are the recommended treatment against pemphigus vulgaris.

D. Methotrexate 15 mg weekly

Methotrexate is an immune suppressant commonly used to treat several dermatological conditions including psoriasis and eczema. However, it is not commonly used in the treatment of pemphigus vulgaris due to a series of publications that linked it to high rates of morbidity and mortality.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with flat pigmented patches over his flanks and gums. He has been treated over the past few months for a pustular rash around his nose. Which of the following drugs is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation:
A. Minocycline

Increased skin pigmentation with blue/black or grey discoloration is rarely seen in patients taking minocycline for a prolonged period. The facial rash may well be rosacea, for which tetracyclines are a standard treatment modality.

D. Co-trimoxazole

Co-trimoxazole is associated with skin rashes and photosensitivity, rather than the hyperpigmentation seen here.

B. Erythromycin

Erythromycin may be associated with skin eruptions, itching and urticaria, not with skin pigmentation.

C. Prednisolone

Prednisolone use over a chronic period is associated with weight gain and skin thinning, rather than the hyperpigmentation seen here.

E. Flucloxacillin

Flucloxacillin is associated with non-specific skin rashes, urticarial and purpura, rather than the blue/black/grey discoloration seen here.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman is seen in the Dermatology Clinic with a new rash. She complains that they can appear overnight and she can predict where the next lesion will appear. They are not itchy but can be mildly painful. Her GP has tried topical emollients and corticosteroids, but the lesions continue to appear. Her past medical history includes anxiety and emotionally unstable personality disorder and she regularly takes propranolol and clonazepam. On examination, she has a well-circumscribed circular-shaped lesion on her left forearm. There are no scaling or exfoliative changes, nor is there any blistering. There are multiple scars of a similar appearance, along with linear scars over both forearms and shins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Dermatitis artefacta

This patient has a likely diagnosis of dermatitis artefacta. Dermatitis artefacta is a skin condition associated with self-inflicted injury from the patient. It is usually secondary to an underlying psychological condition, and the history of anxiety and emotionally unstable personality disorder increases the risk of such a condition. Patients may report that the lesions have 'suddenly appeared' or can 'predict the next lesion'. The prevalence is more common in women and typical lesions are generally well-circumscribed lesions that have a geometric shape that does not fit a specific dermatological condition. Often the lesions will be found on areas of the skin that the patient can reach (eg forearms and legs).

E. Psoriasis

Psoriasis is a reasonable differential diagnosis, given that propranolol is a medication that can exacerbate symptoms of psoriasis. However, the presentation of psoriasis includes inflamed plaques and papules, with a silvery white scale over the extensor surfaces and scalp. However, the lack of scale or progression of lesions makes psoriasis unlikely.

A. Atopic eczema

Atopic eczema is an inflammatory skin disorder characterised by dry, exfoliative skin changes associated with erythema, scaling and pruritis. Although it is a common skin disorder, the findings on this patient's examination are not in keeping with eczema.

C. Erythema multiforme

Erythema multiforme is a self-limiting skin condition associated with annular erythematous skin lesions over the body surface. Typically, the lesions cover less than 10% of the total body surface area. Erythema multiforme is a hypersensitivity reaction and can be triggered by infections, medications and vaccinations. Although this patient has a circular lesion, it is currently only one lesion on the forearm, along with multiple scars of circular and linear shape. This makes dermatitis artefacta more likely the diagnosis.

D. Erythema nodosum

Erythema nodosum is a hypersensitivity reaction that causes tender and erythematous nodules to appear, most commonly over the shins. It is associated with arthralgia, fever and other underlying conditions, for example, inflammatory bowel disease or sarcoidosis. This does not fit with the patient's current presentation.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man is unable to sleep because of an extremely itchy rash. On examination in the Dermatology Clinic, he has violaceous, shiny, flat-topped papules on both wrists, which are particularly marked around an old scar on the flexor aspect of his right forearm. He has recently commenced beta-blocker therapy for control of blood pressure (BP) and to help manage two recent episodes of paroxysmal SVT. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his skin rash?
questions.explanation:
B. Lichen planus

Lichen planus (LP) characteristically affects flexor surfaces, particularly the wrists. There are fine, white streaks on the surface of the lesions if viewed through a hand lens (Wickham's striae). It demonstrates the Koebner phenomenon (as does psoriasis) - a linear pattern along scratch marks or scars. There are often asymptomatic lacy, white lesions in the buccal mucosa. Certain drugs may cause an LP-like eruption, particularly thiazides, β- blockers, phenothiazines, antimalarials and methyldopa. LP usually resolves spontaneously in a few months, but steroids may be required if pruritus is severe.

E. Eruptive xanthomatosis

Eruptive xanthomas occur on extensor surfaces and are associated with severe hypertriglyceridaemia.

A. Guttate psoriasis

Guttate psoriasis is associated with multiple plaques of psoriasis including over the upper body, rather than the limited skin disease seen here.

C. Contact dermatitis

Contact dermatitis is associated with a rash on skin exposed to the allergen, and hence it's most likely to occur on areas such as the hands.

D. Lichen sclerosis

Lichen sclerosis is an itchy scarring rash which most commonly affects the genital area and appears to occur more commonly in women.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic with a three month history of an exquisitely painful ulcer on his right shin. This started after an insect bite and rapidly developed into an ulcer. He has a background of inflammatory bowel disease. The other leg was entirely normal. Which inflammatory cells are most likely to be seen in the ulcer on histological analysis?
questions.explanation:
A. Neutrophils

The diagnosis is pyoderma gangrenosum, which is a neutrophilic dermatosis. Pyoderma gangrenosum is a type of 'neutrophilic dermatosis'. These are conditions characterised by dense infiltrate of neutrophils in the affected tissue. They often arise as a reaction to an underlying systemic illness. They may arise at the site of injury, e.g.

insect bite or needle prick. Other examples of neutrophilic dermatoses include Sweet syndrome, neutrophilic eccrine hidradenitis and erythema elevatum diutinum. Pyoderma gangrenosum is seen with increasing frequency in patients with inflammatory bowel disease.

D. Red blood cells

Haematoma formation with bleeding isn't a primary feature of pyoderma gangrenosum, and red cells are unlikely to be a prominent feature of a biopsy taken from round the edge of a lesion.

B. Lymphocytes

Lymphocytic infiltration occurs in a number of other inflammatory dermatoses, including psoriasis and atopic dermatitis.

C. Eosinophils

Eosinophils are seen across a range of inflammatory skin diseases, including allergic drug eruptions, urticaria, allergic contact dermatitis, atopic dermatitis and eczema.

E. Basophils

Basophils are not a prominent feature of biopsy in inflammatory skin diseases. 39069

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with severe psoriasis which is refractory to treatment with topical steroids is commenced on ciclosporin therapy. He attends the Emergency Department (ED) with a lower respiratory tract infection (RTI). Which of the following antibiotics should be avoided with respect to his treatment?
questions.explanation:
C. Clarithromycin

Macrolide antibiotics can significantly increase ciclosporin concentration and may drive nephrotoxicity in some cases because of inhibition of CYP3A4. Erythromycin can increase ciclosporin exposure 4- to 7-fold, sometimes resulting in nephrotoxicity. Clarithromycin has been reported to double the exposure of ciclosporin. Azitromycin increases ciclosporin levels by around 20%.

E. Doxycycline

Doxycycline is excreted primarily in bile but does not interfere with drugs metabolised by the CYP 3A4 enzyme system.

A. Cephalexin

Cephalexin is renally excreted and has no interaction with the CYP3A4 enzyme system.

B. Ciprofloxacin

Ciprofloxacin is a weak inhibitor of CYP-1A2, which doesn't interfere with ciclosporin metabolism.

D. Co-amoxiclav

Co-amoxiclav is a penicillin and is therefore not metabolised via the P450 system. 38305

questions.question: A 37-year-old Turkish man is referred to the Dermatology Clinic by his General Practitioner (GP) with the 'warty' skin lesion seen below: His girlfriend is worried that it has worsened over the last nine months. He feels that sometimes it completely clears up spontaneously. He has not tried any treatments. It has recently become itchy, and he has been finding sexual intercourse painful. More recently, he has noticed an itchy lesion on the dorsum of his big toe, too. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Lichen planus

Lichen planus is of unknown aetiology. Its association with autoimmune diseases, like vitiligo, alopecia areata and ulcerative colitis, suggests that it too can be mediated immunologically. Typical lesions are violaceous, intensely itchy, flat-topped papules arising on the extremities. The condition can affect the skin and genitalia. In 50% of patients, there are oral lesions, eg white, asymptomatic, lacy lines, dots or plaques. In 10% of patients, there are nail changes, eg longitudinal ridging and destruction of the nail bed. Potent topical steroids are the treatment of choice, but response is variable.

C. Psoriasis

Psoriasis can affect multiple body sites (extensor surfaces, scalp, nails), including the genital skin. Clinically, it is typified by the presence of erythema and scale. However, flexural psoriasis commonly present differently, with shiny, erythematous skin that lacks scaling.

B. Lichen sclerosus

Male genital lichen sclerosus is generally a disease of the uncircumcised, with the weight of evidence indicating that it is due to chronic, intermittent, occluded exposure of a susceptible epithelium to urine. Dyspareunia, itch and a rash are the predominant symptoms. Phimosis is common. Signs can range from subtle to florid and can manifest as shiny, sclerotic patches or patches with telangiectasia and sparse purpura. Circumcision is commonly required when treatment with topical super-potent steroids proves inadequate.

D. Genital warts

Warts can occur on any part of the anogenital area, including the urethra and anus. Unlike warts at other sites that may have a hard, keratinous surface, the genitals present as flesh-coloured papules that may coalesce to form plaques. A tiny black dot may be observed on the surface due to the presence intracorneal haemorrhage.

E. Primary syphilis

Primary syphilis presents with a painless papule and ulcerates (chancre). This heals over a period of 4-8 weeks without any treatment. Untreated syphilis is likely to then progress to the secondary stage with widespread rash and flu-like symptoms.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman, with multiple medical problems including ischaemic heart disease (IHD), chronic kidney disease (CKD), treated hypothyroidism, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and a 60 pack/year smoking history, presents with exquisitely painful, necrotic ulcers on her abdomen, thighs and shins. She says that these ulcers usually begin as areas of blue/black discoloured skin before they break down. A diagnosis of calciphylaxis is confirmed. Which of the following is the most important risk factor for development of her calciphylaxis?
questions.explanation:
B. Chronic kidney disease

Calciphylaxis is a life-threatening condition most often seen in late-stage chronic kidney disease on dialysis.

Calcium deposits in the cutaneous arteries lead to thrombosis and ischaemic necrosis, with refractory ulcers often in the lower extremities, abdomen or buttocks.

E. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

Although SLE is associated with skin ulceration, with respect to calciphylaxis it is kidney disease that is the most important predisposing factor.

A. Venous insufficiency

Venous insufficiency is most strongly associated with varicose eczema and ulceration over the medial malleolus.

C. Smoking

Although smoking increases the risk of necrotic ulcer formation, it isn't the primary cause of calciphylaxis.

D. Hypothyroidism

Hypothyroidism may be associated with hair loss and skin oedema, but isn't associated with ulceration. 38311

questions.question: A 32-year-old man is seen by his General Practitioner (GP) with a long history of anaemia. He denies haematemesis or melaena. His past medical history includes an episode of intussusception one year ago. He has been investigated previously with an upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy and a colonoscopy, which are normal. Lower duodenal biopsies are normal. He has since been started on iron tablets. On examination, the only significant findings are spots on his buccal mucosa and fingers,shown below. Investigations reveal the following: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin (Hb) 91 g/l 135-175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.0 × 10⁹/l 4.0-11.0 × 10⁹/l Platelets (PLT) 192 × 10⁹/l 150-400 × 10⁹/l Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 71 fl 80-100 fl Ferritin 3 µg/l 20-250 µg/l A barium meal and follow-through is abnormal and an enteroscopy shows multiple hamartomatous polyps. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome

Perioral freckling is seen in Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Other areas that may be affected by dark melanin flecks include the fingers, toes and perianal skin. It is an autosomal dominant condition with small intestinal hamartomas and an increased risk of gastrointestinal malignancies. It usually presents in the second or third decade of life and patients may develop anaemia or intussusception. Current surveillance recommendations include annual upper and lower endoscopy plus barium meal and follow-through.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Peutz-Jeghers-Syndrom.JPG (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Peutz-Jeghers-Syndrom.JPG) - This file is licensed under the Creative Commons (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/en:Creative_Commons) Attribution-Share Alike 4.0 International (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/deed.en) license.

A. Gardner syndrome

Gardner syndrome is a form of familial adenomatosis polyposis with osteomas and neuromas. These can especially affect the skull. Like all familial adenomatosis polyposis, monitoring for malignancy is needed.

C. Cowden syndrome

Cowden syndrome is characterised by multiple hamartomas of the skin, mucous membranes, thyroid and breast, associated with hamartomatous polyps of the gastrointestinal and urinary tracts.

D. Familial adenomatosis polyposis

Familial adenomatosis polyposis (FAP) is associated with hundreds to thousands of colonic adenomas. This can cause rectal bleeding and anaemia, and may progress to malignancy. Serial monitoring with colonoscopy is needed.

E. Pseudo-polyps

Pseudo-polyps are projecting masses that occur from scar tissue following repeated healing in bowel ulceration. These can cause bowel obstruction, but not intussusception and would need an underlying inflammatory bowel diagnosis to qualify as a viable differential diagnosis. 7407

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) complaining of a 6-month history of fatigue and mild cough. More recently, she has noticed pain in her ankles, meaning that she struggles with her 1-mile walk to work. She also reports intermittent night sweats, which she has put down to approaching menopause. She is a non-smoker with no past medical history. On examination, her blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg. Her heart rate is 80 bpm and regular. A rash is noticed over the front of her legs, which consists of red, tender nodules. Her GP organises a chest X-ray: What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient's skin rash?
questions.explanation:
C. Erythema nodosum

Erythema nodosum is a type of panniculitis affecting the subcutaneous fat, which usually presents as red, tender nodules. They usually occur over the shins and are bilateral. They can be 3-20 cm in diameter and are commonly associated with joint pain and fever. This patient has also presented with symptoms of sarcoidosis (fatigue and cough) and has bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on her chest X-ray. This patient has Löfgren syndrome - a triad of fever, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and erythema nodosum - which is an acute form of sarcoidosis. Treatment often involves non-steroidal anti-inflammatories, steroids and immunosuppressants.

Compression socks can reduce swelling and discomfort of the erythema nodosum.

Image source: CC by Assoc Prof Craig Hacking, Radiopaedia.

D. Histoid leprosy

Histoid leprosy presents as multiple dome-shaped, skin-coloured to coppery-red papules and nodules which are present on the limbs and trunk. This is due to infection with Mycobacterium leprae which usually occurs in warm, wet areas in the tropics and subtropics. It is an infection of the skin and peripheral nerves, with the usual presenting symptom being numbness, initially to temperature sensation. The clinical signs and symptoms here of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and fever are in keeping with Löfgren syndrome, an acute form of sarcoidosis.

A. Cutaneous lupus erythematosus

Cutaneous lupus erythematosus is a type of connective tissue disease localised to the skin, which can be associated with systemic lupus erythematosus to varying degrees. Clinical features can include a malar butterfly rash localised to the face, diffuse or popular erythema over the face, trunk and limbs and discoid, scaly plaques on the ears, cheeks, nose and scalp. The rash in this scenario is not in keeping with cutaneous lupus erythematosus.

B. Erythema induratum

Erythema induratum, also known as nodular vasculitis, is a type of panniculitis often seen when there is poor circulation to the legs, eg in cold conditions, venous disease and hypertension. Nodules often occur with ulceration over the posterior calves. This patient's rash is affecting the anterior of her legs and she has no risk factors for nodular vasculitis.

E. Traumatic panniculitis

Traumatic panniculitis is an inflammatory condition of the subcutaneous fat, caused by physical or chemical agents. There may have been preceding blunt trauma or a cold injury. The degree of inflammation is usually not related to the degree of trauma. Usually, it presents as a subcutaneous painful plaque, nodule or an ill-defined mass with erythema. There is nothing in this patient's history to suggest that this is the diagnosis. 33406

questions.question: A 40-year-old man presents to his General Practitoner (GP) with an asymptomatic, rash of the dorsum of his foot. On examination, he had multiple pin-point macules and 'cayenne pepper spots'. He tells you he took part in a long-distance run a few days earlier. What is the most likely pathology?
questions.explanation:
C. Capillaritis

Capillaritis (otherwise known as progressive pigmented purpura, or Schamberg's disease) can arise due to exercise, for no known cause, and due to venous insufficiency. It is asymptomatic and has no systemic associations. In this case it is likely to be due to the long-distance run and will resolve over a few days.

D. Livedo reticularis

Livedo reticularis occurs in a net-like, mottled pattern, is more marked in cold weather, and is seen on both upper and lower limbs.

A. Lipodermatosclerosis

Lipodermatosclerosis is painful indurated erythema and occurs in people with chronic venous insufficiency.

B. Necrobiosis lipoidica

Necrobiosis lipoidica consist of well-defined yellow plaques with telangiectasia, atrophic or ulcerated centre and a raised erythematous rim, associated with insulin dependent diabetes.

E. Erythromelalgia

Erythromelalgia is a painful, burning erythema associated with thrombocythaemia.

questions.question: A 26-year-old woman, currently in the second trimester of pregnancy, presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a lesion on her right thumb. This started to develop five weeks ago and has grown rapidly. She remembers getting her thumb caught on a rose bush in the garden. The lesion is not particularly painful, but is a nuisance as it gets caught on clothes and bleeds profusely. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Pyogenic granuloma

Pyogenic granuloma (PG) is a benign vascular skin tumour that commonly presents at the site of a penetrating injury. Pregnancy is a risk factor. There is a history of rapid growth on previously normal skin. A history of a 'mole' at the site, where the lesion arose should alert the clinician to the possibility of alternative diagnoses such as amelanotic malignant melanoma, is common. Commonly used options for treatment include curettage with cautery and cryotherapy.

E. Viral wart

The degree of protuberance seen here would be unusual for a viral wart, as would the speed of growth seen here over only 5 weeks.

A. Pyoderma gangrenosum

Pyoderma gangrenosum is a condition associated with the development of painful, ulcerated, necrotic lesions, seen on the legs and around surgical wounds.

C. Squamous cell carcinoma

Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is rarer and very unlikely to present in a young woman with type 6 skin (Fitzpatrick scale).

Fitzpatrick skin type classification: Skin Type Typical Features Tanning Ability 1 Pale white skin, blue/hazel eyes, blonde/red hair Always burns, does not tan 2 Fair skin, blue eyes Burns easily, tans poorly 3 Darker white skin Tans after initial burn 4 Light brown skin Burns minimally, tans easily 5 Brown skin Rarely burns, tans darkly easily 6 Dark brown or black skin Never burns, always tans darkly

D. Keloid scar

Keloid scars don't protrude and a significant increase in size wouldn't be expected so long after the initial 38521 insult.

questions.question: A 16-year-old girl is referred to the Dermatology Clinic. She is white but has paler skin compared to her parents and siblings. More recently, she has noticed a more significant deterioration in her vision and reports blurred vision and sensitivity to bright light. There is no past medical history or relevant family history of note. On examination, she has global hypopigmentation of all skin surfaces. Her hair is extremely fair and her eyes are a blue-grey colour. There is noticeable nystagmus on testing eye movements and she experiences discomfort in testing pupillary responses to light. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Albinism

This patient has a likely diagnosis of albinism. From the history and examination, she has globally pale skin with fair hair and pale eye colour that is associated with the condition. Furthermore, there are noticeable ocular changes including nystagmus and photosensitivity which are features of oculocutaneous albinism. Visual symptoms are often the most common presenting complaints for patients with albinism. Other ocular features include foveal hypoplasia, photophobia and strabismus. Oculocutaneous albinism is an autosomal-recessive inherited condition that causes a defect or absence of the enzymes involved in the melanin synthesis pathway.

Therefore, the end result is global hypopigmentation secondary to the absence of melanin.

E. Vitiligo

Vitiligo is a reasonable differential diagnosis. Vitiligo is a hypopigmentation skin condition associated with underlying autoimmune conditions such as hypothyroidism and pernicious anaemia. The extent of skin involvement in vitiligo ranges from focal skin involvement to complete pigment loss. However, eye involvement is less common, particularly photophobia and nystagmus.

B. Phenylketonuria

Phenylketonuria is an autosomal-recessive condition secondary to an inborn error of amino-acid metabolism and leads to elevated phenylalanine levels. If this is left untreated, symptoms and signs include intellectual disability and seizures. In the UK, newborns are screened for this condition with the heel prick test.

Dermatological changes include pale skin and eye colour. However, the absence of neurological features makes this diagnosis unlikely.

C. Pityriasis alba

Pityriasis alba is a hypopigmentation skin condition characterised by multiple small hypopigmented lesions over the face, neck, shoulders and upper arms. It is relatively asymptomatic and may resolve after puberty. It does not generally affect eye colour, and the presence of ocular symptoms suggests an alternative diagnosis, such as albinism.

D. Pityriasis versicolor

Pityriasis versicolor is a superficial fungal infection secondary to Malassezia furfur. It causes hypo- or hyperpigmented macules across the trunk and upper extremities. Infection is usually associated with warm and humid environments and oily skin. It would not cause global hyperpigmentation, as seen in this presentation.

questions.question: A 73-year-old woman who has suffered a dense, left-sided hemiplegia is admitted to hosptial from the care home where she lives because the General Practitioner (GP) has noticed a severe sacral pressure ulcer. On examination, you can see a stage 3 pressure ulcer with a great deal of exudative material. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option?
options: E. Leave the sore open to the air
questions.explanation:
D. Alginate based dressing

This lady has exudate material within her pressure ulcer, and therefore she needs an absorptive dressing to avoid build-up of chronic exudate fluid which will affect wound healing. This is the most appropriate option as this dressing forms a gel when it comes into contact with the exudative material. Dressings serve to protect the wound from contamination and facilitate healing by absorbing exudate and protecting healing surfaces. Excess fluid causes wound maceration, while desiccation will slow epithelial cell migration. An absorptive dressing should be used to avoid build-up of chronic wound fluid that can macerate the wound and inhibit cell proliferation and wound healing.

E. Leave the sore open to the air

This will lead to an infection risk and potentially to a build-up of exudate material.

A. Hydrocolloid dressing

Hydrocolloid dressings are useful to prevent bacterial contamination, reduce friction and shear and encourage a moist environment for more rapid healing, but only when there is no substantial exudate. Desiccated wounds lack wound fluids, which provide tissue growth factors to facilitate re-epithelialisation. Healing of pressure- induced injuries is promoted by dressings that maintain a moist wound environment while keeping the surrounding intact skin dry. Choices for a dry wound include saline-moistened gauze, transparent films, hydrocolloids and hydrogels.

B. Gauze dressing

NICE has specifically mentioned that gauze dressing are not to be used to treat pressure ulcers in adults.

C. Foam based dressing

Foam-based dressing will absorb the exudate, but the alginate-based dressing will form a gel that is more likely to promote a warm, moist wound healing environment for grade 2-4 pressure ulcers (as suggested by NICE).

Wound management as advised by NICE: Consider using a dressing for adults that promotes a warm, moist wound healing environment to treat grade 2, 3 and 4 pressure ulcers. Do not offer gauze dressings to treat a pressure ulcer in adults. Do not routinely use topical antiseptics or antimicrobials to treat a pressure ulcer in adults.

GENERAL CARE - The general approach to management of a patient with pressure ulcers should include the following.

Reduce or eliminate underlying contributing factors by providing pressure redistribution with proper positioning and support surfaces.

Provide appropriate local wound care, which may include debridement for patients with necrotic tissue, based on the ulcer's characteristics.

Consider adjunctive therapies, such as negative pressure wound therapy.

Monitor and document the patient's progress.

Provide appropriate psychosocial support.

Reference: Treatment of pressure ulcers: a systematic review. JAMA 2008 Dec 10;300(22):2647-2462. doi: 10.1001/jama.2008.778

questions.question: A 36-year-old man is referred to the Dermatology Clinic by his General Practitioner (GP) with the lesion on his anterior shoulder shown below. He feels it is unsightly and that it may need to be removed. When did the lesion most likely appear?
options: D. Related to sun exposure in the last 10 years
questions.explanation:
B. At onset of puberty

This is a late onset epidermal naevus or birthmark, which occurs mainly in males and is triggered to develop in puberty by circulating androgens. The linear nature of the lesions with evidence of increased pigmentation/keratosis, is more typical of an adolescent onset lesion rather than one which presents at birth.

E. Related to alcohol consumption

Alcohol consumption and smoking have no impact on the growth of late onset epidermal naevi.

A. At birth

Congenital naevi identified at birth tend not to follow the linear pattern seen here, making the lesion less likely to have been present at birth.

C. In the last 2-3 years

As these lesions are related to the puberty related hormone surge and there is no evidence of use of unregulated androgens for body building, it's highly unlikely this man's naevus has worsened over the past 2-3 years.

D. Related to sun exposure in the last 10 years

Excessive skin exposure may result in development of a skin cancer, but the picture here is much more consistent with a benign epidermal naevus.

questions.question: A 47-year-old man is referred to the Medical Clinic for investigation of microcytic anaemia. He has not noticed any symptoms of anaemia and no change to bowel habit, nor any change in his weight. He has a past medical history of frequent epistaxis and asthma. He takes no regular medication but has a salbutamol inhaler. A photograph of his lip is shown below: What investigation would be most appropriate to establish an underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Computed tomography (CT) angiogram bowel

This patient has telangiectasia on his lips with a history of epistaxis, as well as microcytic anaemia suggestive of chronic blood loss. This makes the diagnosis of Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome likely. It is necessary to use CT angiography, or MR angiography, to further identify lesions to establish a diagnosis. Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome is also known as hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, and is an autosomal dominant condition characterised by vascular dysplasia leading to telangiectasia, as well as increased frequency of arteriovenous malformations, particularly of the gastrointestinal tract, lungs, liver and brain.

B. Clotting screen

A. clotting screen would be more likely to be helpful in diagnosis in a patient with a haemophilia. That would be

been suggested by a history of easy bruising or bleeding, or spontaneous internal bleeding such as haemarthrosis.

C. Liver function tests

Liver function would be more useful if there were evidence of chronic liver failure or a cause of chronic liver disease. In patients with end-stage liver disease, there can be increased frequency towards bleeding and abnormal clotting. There can also be venous congestion, but this normally manifests as spider naevi.

D. Anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibodies

Anti-neutrophil cytoplasm antibodies would be a useful first-line investigation in various autoimmune conditions, such as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis. However, there is a lack of clinical features such as eosinophilia or kidney disease to suggest either diagnosis.

E. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) testing

This patient does not have any risk factors for HIV nor has any evidence of an acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS)-defining illness. Had there been evidence of hairy cell leukoplakia then HIV testing would be an appropriate first-line investigation. This would have been suggested by white plaques on the sides of the tongue.

questions.question: An 18-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with recurrent episodes of skin lesions for the past six months. The patient was not on any medications and she used a barrier method for contraception. On examination, there are multiple lesions which are thick, greasy, yellowish-white scales over the scalp, eyebrows, side of the nose and ears. There are no other lesions on other parts of the body. Which of the following should be used to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
D. Selenium sulfide

This patient is likely suffering from seborrhoeic dermatitis. Selenium sulfide is a keratolytic and an antifungal agent and is used in the form of shampoos and stay-on lotions in the management of seborrhoeic dermatitis.

E. Zinc emollients

Zinc emollients are useful in relieving symptoms of eczematous skin conditions. They are not used to treat seborrhoeic dermatitis.

A. Acitretin

Acitretin is used in psoriasis (mainly pustular and erythrodermic variants). This patient has features characteristic of seborrhoeic dermatitis, so acitretin would not be appropriate here.

B. Ciclosporin

Ciclosporin is an immunosuppressant used in the management of diseases such as erythrodermic psoriasis. It is not used in the management of seborrhoeic dermatitis.

C. Ivermectin

Ivermectin is used in the management of scabies, which may present with vesicular or pustular lesions in the interdigital areas and associated with severe pruritus which worsens in the night.

questions.question: A 36-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with the following rash, which first appeared three days ago. Which of the following is most associated with this skin rash?
questions.explanation:
B. Mycoplasma infection

This man has erythema multiforme. He shows the classical target lesions. These have three zones: a central area of dusky erythema, a middle paler zone of oedema and an outer erythematous ring. The lesions preferentially involve the extremities and trunk. They usually appear in successive crops and fade in 1-2 weeks.

There are multiple triggering factors, although the cause is not determined in up to 50% of cases. The most common association is with preceding herpes simplex or mycoplasma infection, although drugs such as sulphonamides and penicillins are also frequently implicated.

C. Orf

Orf is a parapox virus transmitted by sheep and goats; although it is a cause of erythema multiforme, it is a less common cause than mycoplasma infection.

A. Crohn's disease

Crohn's disease is associated with a number of skin manifestations, including erythema nodosum and pyoderma gangrenosum.

D. Tuberculosis

Like Crohn's disease, tuberculosis is associated with erythema nodosum rather than the erythema multiforme seen here.

E. Alcoholism

Alcoholism is associated with guttate psoriasis, which leads to discrete erythematous scaling lesions rather than the target lesions seen here.

questions.question: A 20-year-old man, who has just returned from holidays in Canada, presents to his General Practitioner (GP) as he has just developed the rash shown below. He tells you that he has been walking in the mountains, wearing shorts for most of his holiday: Given the suspected diagnosis, what is the correct treatment choice if he feels otherwise well?
questions.explanation:
D. Oral doxycycline

The rash represents erythema chronicum migrans. This starts as a small papule and develops into a slow- enlarging ring with a raised border and central clearance. It is pathognomonic of Lyme disease and is caused by the spirochaete Borrelia burgdorferi.

A. single dose of doxycycline 200 mg is effective prophylaxis after a tick bite if given within 72 hours. If not, 14-

21 days of treatment is necessary.

A. Clotrimazole cream

Clotrimazole cream is an antifungal agent commonly used in the treatment of superficial fungal infections. This history here is not consistent with a a fungal infection.

B. Topical beclomethasone cream

Topical steroids do not have a role in the management of erythema chronicum migrans, which is the most likely diagnosis due to the characteristic rash seen here.

C. Oral ketoconazole

Like clotrimazole, this is an antifungal agent and would not be effective against Lyme disease, the most likely diagnosis due to the history and typical rash as seen here.

E. Intravenous (IV) benzylpenicillin

If the patient has any late complications (meningitis, cranial nerve palsies, heart block, arthropathy), then high- dose IV benzylpenicillin or cefotaxime is warranted.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman attends the Dermatology Outpatients Clinic with an enlarging, asymptomatic mole on her abdomen. She is otherwise fit and healthy and does not take any regular medications. Examination revealed the lesion shown below. What is the most appropriate management option in this case?
options: B. Incisional biopsy through the centre of the lesion
C. Excisional biopsy with 5mm clinical margins
D. Excisional biopsy with at least 1 cm clinical margins
E. Excisional biopsy, followed by chemotherapy
questions.explanation:
D. Excisional biopsy with at least 1 cm clinical margins

An excisional/complete biopsy of suspicious lesions with 1-3 mm margin of normal skin and extending to a depth to encompass the thickest portion of the lesion is the preferred technique and should be performed whenever possible. Narrow margin excision allows for the assessment of the entire lesion without compromising subsequent, wider surgery or potential staging with the sentinel lymph node biopsy technique. If melanoma is detected then further surgical resection is required.

For Melanoma in situ 0.5 to 1cm resection margin is recommended. For Melanoma, 1 cm resection margin if Breslow thickness < 1 mm , 1-2 cm margin if > 1 to 2 mm breslow thickness and > 2 cm margin if > 2 mm thickness is advised.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Melanoma.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Melanoma.jpg) - Public domain

C. Excisional biopsy with 5mm clinical margins

Following histological diagnosis of a melanoma, further wide local excision is recommended with surgical margins dependant on Breslow thickness.

A. Re-assurance

The lesion displayed shows features suggestive of a melanoma (asymmetry, shape irregularity, multiple colours, diameter larger than 6mm, and associated with a history of growth) and should not be left untreated.

B. Incisional biopsy through the centre of the lesion

Suspicious lesions, such as the one shown here, need to be excised rather than sampled with incisional biopsy.

However, sampling suspicious areas may be indicated in large lesions, particularly those on the face.

E. Excisional biopsy, followed by chemotherapy

Not all melanomas require treatment with chemotherapy. Management is variable and depends on Breslow thickness. Decisions should be taken by the local multidisciplinary team meeting. Patients with high-risk melanomas or those with evidence of local lymphadenopathy should be investigated with CT scanning and may be considered for treatment with chemotherapy or immunotherapy.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man, who is known to suffer with anxiety and depression, presents to his General Practitioner (GP) with a chronic, intensely itchy, erythematous patch on his lower leg, shown below. He recognises and admits that the rash is more pronounced and painful after itching. There are no other skin problems noted elsewhere, and he has no other significant health problems. Routine bloods are unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
C. Lichen simplex et chronicus

Lichen simplex et chronicus occurs when the skin becomes thickened and leathery (lichenified) because of chronic rubbing - sometimes a stress related habit. It favours the calf, nape of the neck and vulval/peri-anal skin.

The localised nature of this, coupled with the lack of other systemic features, further support the underlying diagnosis.

B. Delusional parasitosis

Delusional parasitosis is a fixed, false belief that there is an infestation with insect or parasite and is much more likely to result in generalised symptoms.

A. Dysmorphophobia

Dysmorphophobia is an altered perception of one's appearance and a belief that there is a flaw in appearance.

In some cases, this may result in inappropriate plastic surgery to alter appearance.

D. Dermatitis artefacta

Dermatitis artefacta is associated with self-mutilation, usually denied by the patient, and may appear overnight.

E. Shingles

Shingles is an acutely painful vesicular rash, rather than the chronic itchy lesion seen here.

questions.question: A 19-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a 3-hour history of rectal bleeding and lower abdominal pain. There is no past medical history of note, although she reports that her mother used to have similar problems with rectal bleeding, requiring blood transfusions and hospitalisation. The appearance of her mouth is shown below: On colonoscopy, she is found to have multiple colonic polyps. An upper GI tract endoscopy reveals no significant abnormality. How often should upper GI endoscopy be repeated in this patient?
options: E. Only if she has symptoms
questions.explanation:
C. 3-yearly

The perioral pigmentation here is consistent with a diagnosis of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is caused by mutations in either the SMAD4 or the BMPR1A gene, with SMAD4 mutations less likely to lead to upper GI cancers. Current surveillance guidelines state that if an abnormality is found on either colonoscopy or upper GI endoscopy, both imaging studies should be repeated in three years.

B. Yearly

Yearly endoscopy is incorrect. Surveillance guidelines recommend that endoscopies and colonoscopies are repeated 3-yearly if polyps are found.

A. 6-monthly

Even if polyps were identified on upper GI tract endoscopy, 6-monthly endoscopy is excessively frequent and may drive inappropriate use of resources while increasing patient anxiety.

D. 5-yearly

Given the aetiology of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, waiting for five years for repeat upper GI endoscopy risks the development of a gastric or oesophageal cancer in the intervening period.

E. Only if she has symptoms

Given the late presentation of upper GI cancers and the significant risk of tumour development in patients with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, an expectant strategy is unacceptable.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old man was referred to the Immunology Department of a tertiary hospital with repeated episodes of intermittent facial flushing, diarrhoea and breathlessness for the past two years. Physical examination revealed multiple polymorphic lesions over the trunk and limbs, which increased in size and became erythematous within minutes of rubbing, scratching or stroking. A picture of the patient's back is taken:
InvestigationResultNormal Value
Haemoglobin (Hb)134 g/L135–175 g/L
White cell count (WCC)9.2 ×10⁹/L4–11 ×10⁹/L
Neutrophils6.2 ×10⁹/L2.5–7.58 ×10⁹/L
Lymphocytes2.8 ×10⁹/L1.5–3.5 ×10⁹/L
Eosinophils0.2 ×10⁹/L0–0.4 ×10⁹/L
Platelet count277 ×10⁹/L150–400 ×10⁹/L
Total immunoglobulin E (IgE)840 IU/mL150–300 IU/mL
Serum tryptase15 ng/mL<10 ng/mL
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
B. Cutaneous mastocytosis

The most likely diagnosis is mastocytosis and it frequently presents in young patients with the presence of polymorphic lesions of maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis, known as urticaria pigmentosa. Some may experience flushing, nausea/vomiting or diarrhoea. Infants may have episodic blistering. These clinical features, along with an elevated IgE level and slightly raised serum tryptase level, are suggestive of cutaneous mastocytosis. There are no therapies that alter the natural course of cutaneous mastocytosis, and management involves avoiding triggers of mast cell degranulation, along with pharmacotherapy, for symptomatic relief.

Annual monitoring is required, and abnormalities of complete blood count or elevation of serum tryptase level > 20 ng/ml should trigger an evaluation for systemic mastocytosis.

Image credit: CC BY-SA 4.0 Doc James.

https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mastocytosis2019.jpg

D. Juvenile xanthogranuloma

Juvenile xanthogranuloma presents as a reddish or yellowish to brown papule, plaque or nodule and is usually solitary.

A. Acne vulgaris

This patient's clinical presentation and laboratory evaluation are suggestive of cutaneous mastocytosis as acne vulgaris typically presents with comedones.

C. Idiopathic urticaria

The presence of pre-existing lesions, a positive Darier sign (increase in size of lesions with stroking) and slightly raised tryptase levels point towards a diagnosis of cutaneous mastocytosis.

E. Solid mast cell tumours

Solid mast cell tumours are extremely rare and usually have abnormalities in the WCC.

questions.question: A 76-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with intermittent pain over her upper left chest. She has suffered a weeping vesicular rash over the area for the past four days associated with a burning pain. There is a history of chicken pox infection as a child. On examination, there is a well-demarcated rash consisting of dried-up crusted and healing vesicles, corresponding to one dermatome. Which of the following options represents the most appropriate treatment in this patient?
questions.explanation:
D. Gabapentin

It is clear that this patient has suffered an unpleasant attack of Herpes zoster reactivation, also known as shingles. At this stage though, with crusting, dried-up and healing lesions there is no value in antiviral therapy.

Gabapentin is a useful oral agent to block the pain associated with post-herpetic neuralgia; 300 mg daily is the most appropriate starting dose, with effective doses being from 900 mg upwards, and it can be increased up to 3.6 g/day. Alternatives include tricyclic anti-depressants and topical capsaicin cream.

E. IV aciclovir

This is most appropriate for HSV encephalitis. In HSV encephalitis there is spread from cranial nerve ganglia to frontal and temporal lobes, leading to headaches, behavioural change, fever, fits and headaches.

A. Aciclovir ointment

This is mostly useful against conjunctival varicella zoster, where there is dermatomal distribution within the trigeminal nerve and including the eye.

B. Oral aciclovir

Antiviral therapy should be administered in herpes zoster after 72 hours if new lesions are appearing at the time of presentation, as this indicates ongoing viral replication. However, the clinical utility of initiating antiviral therapy more than 72 hours after the onset of lesions in immunocompetent persons is unknown. There is likely minimal benefit of antiviral therapy in the patient who has lesions that have encrusted. Hence in this patient aciclovir will not be beneficial.

C. Oral valciclovir

Valciclovir is an alternative option to acyclovir, with good cover against herpes viruses. 33185

questions.question: A 19-year-old man attends the Dermatology Clinic with a nine month history of a lesion on the head of his penis. He is very embarrassed by the appearance. He says that he has a skin condition affecting various other parts of his body. The lesion does not cause severe symptoms, but can be a little sore and itchy at times. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
A. Psoriasis

This condition is relatively common in the genital area. It gives rise to well-defined, erythematous scaly plaques.

Eczema can appear very similar, though the discoid form tends to be very itchy. In this situation, skin changes should be sought elsewhere. A mild- or moderate-potency topical corticosteroid cream would be appropriate initial treatment on the genital area.

B. Discoid eczema

Whilst this also presents with well-defined, scaly plaques, it is unusual on the genital area and tends to be intensely pruritic.

C. Lichen planus

This condition classically presents with violaceous pruritic papules.

D. Lichen sclerosus

Urologists often refer to this condition as balanitis xerotica obliterans. It is usually confined to genital skin but almost never occurs after circumcision. It usually presents with pale, atrophic skin. Pruritus is variable; painful fissures may occur.

E. Vitiligo

Whilst the penis is a common site for this condition, it manifests as asymptomatic, depigmented macules. 6291

questions.question: A 25-year-old Indian student comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. He has several hypopigmented areas on his lower limbs which were initially a few cm across but over time appear to have coalesced to form a larger area of de-pigmented skin, as shown below. The depigmentation appears to be non-scarring. He has no past medical history of note and takes no regular medication. The skin areas appear yellow-green in colour under Wood's light. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.explanation:
C. Topical Corticosteroids

The answer is Topical Corticosteroids - The most likely diagnosis is vitiligo, which shows blue-white or yellow-green under Wood's light. For limited disease on the body topical corticosteroids may be adequate, with topical calcineurin inhibitors an option where the response to steroids is poor. For patients with severe progressive disease, systemic therapies are an option, although the risks are usually thought to outweigh potential benefits.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vitiligo.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vitiligo.jpg) - This file is licensed under the Creative Commons (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/en:Creative_Commons) Attribution-Share Alike 4.0 International (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/), 3.0 Unported (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by- sa/3.0/deed.en), 2.5 Generic (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.5/deed.en), 2.0 Generic (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0/deed.en) and 1.0 Generic (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/1.0/deed.en) license.

D. Topical Griseofulvin

Topical Griseofulvin, is incorrect, this is a treatment for tinea corporis, not the diagnosis here, because of the lack of skin scaling and the difference in colour under Wood's lamp.

A. Oral Corticosteroids

Oral Corticosteroids is incorrect, these are not indicated for limited vitiligo, the diagnosis here.

B. Oral Terbinafine

Oral Terbinafine is incorrect, it can be considered for tinea corporis, which looks blue-green, dull yellow or dull blue under Wood's lamp.

E. Topical Ketoconazole

Topical Ketoconazole is incorrect, this is a treatment for tinea corporis, not the diagnosis here, because of the lack of skin scaling and the difference in colour under Wood's lamp.

questions.question: A 23-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with complaints of multiple swollen lesions over the groin, perianal region and axillae for the past six months. He gives a history of persistent discharge from his skin swellings. There was no prior history of anal intercourse or unsafe sexual practice. He did not give any previous history of surgery. Physical examination of the axilla showed skin lesions, shown in the image below. What is the first line of management for this patient?
questions.explanation:
E. Oral tetracycline

The location and characteristics of the skin lesions in this patient are suggestive of hidradenitis suppurativa.

Oral tetracyclines, such as doxycycline or lymecycline, are used as first-line therapy for at least 12 weeks for people with hidradenitis suppurativa.

Image credit: CC BY-SA 4.0 Samuel Freire da Silva.

https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hidradenitis.png

D. Oral clindamycin/rifampicin

Combination treatment with oral clindamycin 300 mg twice daily and rifampicin 300 mg twice daily for 10-12 weeks is used in patients with hidradenitis suppurativa who are unresponsive to tetracyclines.

A. Acitretin

Acitretin is used in men with hidradenitis suppurativa who are unresponsive to antibiotic-based regimens. It should not be used in women of childbearing age due to its teratogenic potential.

B. Adalimumab

Adalimumab is used in people with moderate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa that is unresponsive to conventional therapy.

C. Dapsone

Dapsone is used in patients with hidradenitis suppurativa who are unresponsive to antibiotic-based therapies.

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) with a one day history of a vesicular rash. It is intensely painful and she had been taking maximal paracetamol and ibuprofen tablets to no avail. There are no other areas of rash apart from this. What is the most appropriate management choice?
questions.explanation:
A. Oral aciclovir

The history and position of the rash is suggestive of shingles (herpes zoster). Due to her early presentation, oral aciclovir may help shorten the duration and severity of the episode. Initiation of antiviral therapy as early as possible in the course of acute zoster, and definitely within 72 h of onset, has been shown to be effective in alleviating acute pain and preventing post-herpetic neuralgia (PHN) in most patients.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ShinglesDay1.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:ShinglesDay1.jpg) - public domain

D. Topical clotrimazole

Clotrimazole is an anti-fungal agent; there is nothing in this patient's presentation to suggest that she has a fungal infection. Instead, her symptoms and signs are more consistent with shingles (herpes zoster) for which the appropriate treatment is oral aciclovir. Oral aciclovir has also been shown to reduce pain acutely and to help prevent PHN.

B. Oral opiates

This patient has signs and symptoms suggestive of shingles (herpes zoster). Opioid analgesia is unlikely to help with her pain, but treatment of the underlying condition with oral aciclovir can be effective in alleviating acute pain and it may prevent PHN.

C. Topical aciclovir

This patient does have shingles (herpes zoster), but oral, not topical, aciclovir is the appropriate treatment. Early treatment with oral aciclovir has been shown to reduce acute pain and help prevent post-herpetic neuralgia.

E. Topical hydrocortisone

Topical hydrocortisone can be useful in itchy skin conditions, but this patient has signs and symptoms suggestive of shingles (herpes zoster). Hydrocortisone would not be an appropriate treatment - instead oral aciclovir should be started, as this can both relieve acute pain and help to prevent PHN.

questions.question: A 23-year-old woman has recently emigrated to the UK from Romania. She presents for the first time to the Medical Clinic in the UK. She does not have a complete medical history but has been concerned by nodules on her back. These have been present for a long time but have not significantly bothered her. She was separated from her family at a young age and so is unsure if any other family member has a similar problem. She has no medical history as far as she is aware. She has had one child, who is healthy. She does not take any regular tablets. A photograph of the nodules on her back is shown below: Further examination of her skin reveals no other abnormalities. What would be the most appropriate step to help establish a diagnosis at this stage?
questions.explanation:
C. Slit lamp examination

This patient likely has neurofibromatosis type 1 as there are multiple neurofibromas on her back. The lack of previous medical involvement explains the lack of a diagnosis at her age. There are seven cardinal clinical features of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1) defined by the National Institutes of Health (NIH). These require two of the following features: • café-au-lait spots: six or more of 15 mm in diameter • neurofibromas: two or more • axillary or inguinal freckling • optic glioma • Lisch nodules: two or more (slit lamp examination) • osseous lesion • family history: first-degree relative with established diagnosis.

Neurofibromatosis type 2 typically presents with progressively worsening hearing loss, tinnitus or balance problems, as well as tumours of the central nervous system. Neurofibromatosis type 2 is subtler than type 1 as there is greater paucity of café-au-lait spots and neurofibromas are less common. Lisch nodules may be seen with a direct ophthalmoscope if the nodules are large or numerous and the iris is light in colour, but the slit lamp is a more reliable way to distinguish Lisch nodules from iris nevi, which are not associated with NF1.

These lesions are detected in fewer than 10 percent of affected children younger than six years of age but are seen in greater than 90 percent of adults.

D. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) testing

This patient has multiple neurofibromas. These are not due to immunosuppression, and the presence of them as chronic lesions reinforces that this is not due to opportunistic infection. If there had been widespread dermal tumour secondary to viral infection, such as multiple warts, then this would be appropriate.

A. Computed tomography (CT) head

Patients with neurofibromatosis type 1 are prone to several neurological complications. Patients can develop epilepsy, glial tumours and schwannomas. Abnormalities can be detected with CT, but this should be done in the presence of symptoms such as headaches or seizures.

B. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) head

An MRI of the brain would be more useful for the diagnosis of optic nerve glioma it allows visualization of the entire course of the optic nerve.

It also helps in the diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 2 as this could help demonstrate unilateral or bilateral schwannomas. It would also be appropriate when assessing for other soft tissue lesions.

E. Karyotyping

Neurofibromatosis is not a disorder linked to chromosomal non-dysjunction, and therefore this would not be a useful investigation.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man presents with scaly, erythematous plaques on the dorsal surfaces of his hands and feet and around his nose and ears. He reports these lesions have been slowly worsening over the past few months. He also describes unintentional weight loss and fatigue. Physical examination reveals hyperkeratotic, violaceous plaques on his distal extremities and perioral area. There are no other systemic symptoms or evidence of infection. What is the underlying mechanism of acrokeratosis paraneoplastica?
options: A. Immune complex deposition in dermal blood vessels
B. Direct keratinocyte hyperproliferation due to viral infection
C. Paraneoplastic syndrome associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the upper digestive tract
D. Autoimmune attack on skin fibroblasts
E. Genetic mutation in the keratin gene
questions.explanation:
C. Paraneoplastic syndrome associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the upper digestive tract

Acrokeratosis paraneoplastica, also known as Bazex syndrome, is a rare paraneoplastic syndrome strongly associated with squamous cell carcinomas of the upper digestive tract (eg pharynx, larynx, oesophagus). The skin findings are considered a response to tumour antigens. Recognition of this syndrome is important for early cancer detection, as skin findings may precede the diagnosis of malignancy by months.

E. Genetic mutation in the keratin gene

Genetic mutations in keratin genes can lead to conditions such as epidermolysis bullosa and other keratinopathies. However, acrokeratosis paraneoplastica is a paraneoplastic syndrome rather than a genetic skin disorder.

A. Immune complex deposition in dermal blood vessels

This mechanism is commonly seen in vasculitis but is not associated with acrokeratosis paraneoplastica, which is primarily a paraneoplastic phenomenon.

B. Direct keratinocyte hyperproliferation due to viral infection

Viral infections, such as those with human papillomavirus, can lead to hyperkeratotic skin lesions. However, acrokeratosis paraneoplastica is not due to viral infections or direct keratinocyte proliferation.

D. Autoimmune attack on skin fibroblasts

While autoimmune reactions can cause various skin manifestations, acrokeratosis paraneoplastica is not an autoimmune process targeting fibroblasts.

questions.question: A 54-year-old man with severe, widespread, chronic plaque psoriasis and arthritis in both hands has failed to respond adequately to treatment with increasing doses of oral methotrexate. He has previously failed treatment with phototherapy, cyclosporine and multiple topical agents. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: B. Switch to treatment with acitretin
questions.explanation:
D. Switch to adalimumab

In severe plaque psoriasis, treatment with biologic agents is available in patients that have previously failed treatment with methotrexate, ciclosporin and phototherapy. Adalimumab is a biologic agent that has been used in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. It acts as a TNF-α (tumour necrosis factor-alpha) antagonist with a good safety profile. However, TNF- α antagonists have been linked to a risk of reactivation of TB and therefore it is important to exclude cases of TB prior to commencing therapy. This is usually done with a chest X-ray and a quantiferon test.

E. Switch to oral prednisolone

Oral corticosteroids are commonly avoided in the treatment of psoriasis due the high likelihood of severe recurrence of symptoms after treatment is discontinued.

A. Switch to subcutaneous methotrexate

Subcutaneous methotrexate is thought to have comparable efficacy to that of oral methotrexate and is often used in an attempt to bypass the gastrointestinal side effects that can be associated by taking oral methotrexate.

B. Switch to treatment with acitretin

Acitretin is an oral retinoid (vitamin-A derivative) that is used in the treatment of severe psoriasis, and in particular pustular psoriasis, erythrodermic psoriasis and psoriasis affecting hands and feet. However, it is not effective against psoriatic arthritis and therefore an alternative agent should be sought in this particular instance.

C. Repeat course of phototherapy

This patient has previously failed to respond to phototherapy and therefore repeated courses are unlikely to mount an improved response.

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) complaining of conjunctivitis affecting her left eye. Apparently, she has suffered from multiple episodes of red eye over the past few years, which correspond to periods of stress or when she is run-down. The appearance of the eye is shown below. Fluorescein staining demonstrates a dendritic ulcer. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her eye problem?
questions.explanation:
B. Herpes simplex infection

Recurrent conjunctivitis with formation of a dendritic ulcer raises the possibility of herpes simplex infection. The image shows small vesicles around the lid margin in keeping with the diagnosis. Where there is epithelial keratitis and ulcer formation, topical antivirals such as aciclovir are the usual initial intervention.

Image source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Herpes_simplex_Lid.jpg (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Herpes_simplex_Lid.jpg) - This file is licensed under the Creative Commons (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/en:Creative_Commons) Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 Unported (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/deed.en) license.

E. Staphylococcus aureus

Staphylococcal conjunctivitis may be milder than bacterial conjunctivitis caused by Gram-negative pathogens; dendritic ulcers are not seen as a feature of the condition.

A. Chlamydia trachomatis

Chlamydia leads to bacterial conjunctivitis rather than the picture here with ulcer formation.

C. Herpes zoster infection

Herpes zoster eye infection is associated with vesicle formation along the affected branch of the ophthalmic nerve, rather than infection being isolated to the eye.

D. Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Pseudomonas is a rare cause of bacterial conjunctivitis. It is an environmental pathogen and is usually only seen as a cause of conjunctivitis where there is an artificial implant within the eye.
